subtopic: MR. BLENKARN-SUGGESTED IRREGULARITY IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (B)-RULING BY MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Perhaps 1 could deal with a point of order which was raised by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) on November 17. The Hon. Member raised a point of order with regard to procedural acceptability of Vote 6b under Consumer and Corporate Affairs in Supplementary Estimates (B) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1984. I was unable to deal with this matter earlier because, as Hon. Members will recall, Supplementary Estimates (B) were referred to committees on November 3, 1983 and were not before the House.
As has been noted before, however, it is helpful to the Chair that there be adequate time to study points of order on the Estimates and the Chair appreciated the courtesy of the Hon. Member in raising the matter when he did. The House will also recall that the Chair wished to extend an opportunity to Hon. Members to rebut or add to the procedural argument. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), on November 24, did make a further contribution. I wish to express my thanks to both Hon. Members who were most helpful to the Chair when considering this important matter.
In presenting his case, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South referred to Section 29 of the Canada Post Corporation Act. He submitted that no authority is given to the Government to seek an appropriation other than "an appropriation to pay losses" and that therefore no legislative authority exists for the appropriation expressed in Vote 6b.
In support of this submission the Hon. Member quotes from the Chair's decision of June 12, 1981, at page 10546 of Debates, stating, in part:
the Government may not, by the use of an Appropriation Act, obtain authority which it does not already have under existing legislation.
I have examined both the Supplementary Estimates (B) and the relevant legislation with respect to the Hon. Member's point of order. The Canada Post Corporation Act states, in part, in Subsection 29(1):
Where at any time the available revenues of the Corporation are insufficient to pay all the operating and income charges of the Corporation as and when due... The Minister of Finance may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, place at the disposal of the Corporation such amounts as may be required ... to meet all such charges.
Subsection 29(2) provides a mechanism for reimbursement of the Treasury for such sums and Subsection 29(3) provides as follows:
Where the annual revenues ... are insufficient for the purposes of Subsection (2) the Minister shall cause the amount of the insufficiency to be included, in the form of a deficit appropriation item, in the next Appropriation Act laid before Parliament thereafter.
Hon. Members will note that the Act refers to "operating and income charges" which the annual revenues are not adequate to cover.
1 would now invite the attention of Hon. Members to Vote 6b at pages 32 and 33 of the Supplementary Estimates (B) in which the "Objects of Expenditure" is described as being for "operating" the Corporation. Such a payment was specifically envisaged under Section 29 of the Act.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South suggested in his submission that the Act did not give the Government the authority to make such a payment because it refers to "activities that have nothing to do with losses". However, the relevant section of the enabling legislation makes no mention of losses but deals only with the insufficiency of revenues to cover operating and income charges. Furthermore, Hon. Members will find that a payment to cover similar operating expenditures was made to the Canada Post Corporation under Consumer and Corporate Affairs Vote 6c in the Appropriation Act No. 4, 1982-83.
In the opinion of the Chair, the Government is seeking to make a payment which is specifically provided for in the Act, and in presenting such an appropriation the Government is not seeking to enlarge its legislative authority. I therefore find that the point of order raised by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South is not well taken and that Consumer and Corporate Affairs Vote 6b is procedurally in order.
In closing, I again wish to express my gratitude to both Members for their valuable assistance.

That this House agrees without reservation with the prediction of the Prime Minister made on August 13, 1969, in a nationally televised press conference when he said, "We'd soon be on the road to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control" and calls upon the Government to initiate policies which would avoid the Prime Minister's prediction.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is an extremely serious one. It is really at the heart of our well being and that of our children tomorrow. It has to do with the last 14 years of extravagant and wasteful spending after the warnings given to the nation back in 1968-69 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
Before I belonged to a political party, I was most impressed with the words of the Prime Minister at that time. The words that really got to me are these, and I quote as follows:
This process of making choices among the myriad of claims and demands on our resources in the context of business enterprise and Government is often referred to as planning and priorities. It is not really very different than the process that each of us in our own lives, whether as individuals or as family units, have to go through. If an individual fails to plan in a coherent way he will soon find that he has run out of resources and has left many urgent things undone. He may find that his children's education is neglected or the medical bills are left unpaid because he has taken an expensive holiday or purchased a red convertible.
Governments are really no different than individuals in this respect and they too must engage in solid planning and to ensure that their scarce resources are being applied to the most urgent and useful purposes.
He went on to say, Mr. Speaker:
Perhaps the most startling fact to emerge from this review is that almost without exception this decade has been characterized by yearly budgetary deficits exceeding $4 billion in total and requiring upwards of $300 million per annum to service.
And he is speaking of the decade of the 1960s. It is easy to see from the sincerity and wisdom of those remarks back on August 13, 1969 that the Prime Minister was as aware then as some of us in this House are today of the seriousness of the behaviour of the Liberal Government over the last 14 years. Back in 1968-69, in the budget address, Mr. Edgar Benson said on October 22, 1968:
We intend to continue severe restraint upon those direct expenditure programs under the Government's control, eliminating what is obsolete, and permitting only the degree of growth that is essential.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, spending on a national accounts basis was $12.6 billion. The annual deficit was $491 million and net debt at the start of that fiscal year was $17.7 billion. On August 13, 1969 the Prime Minister said to the nation on a television broadcast, Mr. Speaker-which is the object of our motion today-and 1 quote:
We'd be on the road to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control.
That year our spending on a national accounts basis was $13.8 billion, and the Prime Minister bragged about that surplus of $493 million. The net debt was at $18 billion. That is the starting point of our debate today.
In 1970-71, at the Liberal policy convention on November 20, 1970, the same Prime Minister said:
You know, anyone can say, "why don't you do more? The answer is the same answer as always, there are competing claims on the economy.
In the meantime our spending had gone up $2 billion in that one year. There was no longer a surplus but a deficit of $372 million, and the net debt had slightly tapered down from $18 billion to $17.6 billion. Following that was the Benson budget speech of 1971-72, in which Mr. Benson said:
We have continuously appealed to Canadian governments, business and the labour movement to be modest in their demands and not demand more from the economy than is coming to them in increased productivity.
Every year I have been in this House, for the past nine and one half years, Sir, we have heard that the only way out of the spending and inflation dilemma is through improved national productivity. We were then still spending $18 billion. We then had doubled our annual deficit to $700 million and our net debt was up to $ 18 billion.
The year 1971-72, was the year of "a buck is a buck is a buck", that great promise of equity and distribution and equality for all. The Hon. John Turner in his budget address of 1972-73, said:
The bare fact of the matter is that we cannot do everything at once. We simply don't have the resources. There are limits to the scope of fiscal policy. There are limits to stimulus and readjustment.
We have now gone up $2.8 billion in spending. We have now moved from a $700 million to almost a $1 billion annual deficit, and our net debt has moved up $800 million.
Then we jump to 1973-74. We had the same Mr. Turner as Minister of Finance, and in his budget address of November 18, 1974, he said:

We have sought and shall continued to seek to cut out waste, to place limits on the growth of the public service and to approve only the most essential new programs.
We have now moved from $20.8 billion Government spending to $30.8 billion in two years. We moved from a $1 billion deficit to a $1.7 billion deficit and our net debt had moved from $18.8 billion to $21.2 billion. The rhetoric was there, Mr. Speaker. They knew exactly what was needed if this nation was to remain healthy and inflation did not reach excessive amounts which would harm the well-being of the elderly, the sick and the youth emerging from our educational system. 1 can remember Mr. Turner standing in the House and saying that the thing he was proudest of was the million jobs he created as Minister of Finance. Where are those jobs, Mr. Speaker? As we stand here today we have two million unemployed. Where are those jobs from "old blue eyes" which started us on this spending spiral?
Then we move into Mr. Macdonald's period of budgetary extravagances; he moved our annual deficit from $6 billion to $10.8 billion. Then we got that gem of them all, Mr. Mac-Eachen. He moved us from a deficit of $11.5 billion to $13.6

billion, and by the time we got to 1982-83 we had gone to a $24.6 billion deficit. Throughout this period of time we heard the rhetoric of these Ministers of Finance and the Prime Minister. They knew exactly what had to be done to manage the country's economy for the wellbeing of the people. But nowhere were they able to deliver what they said they would deliver. Instead we have the situation where today this institution is no longer relevant to two-thirds of the people in Canada because they can no longer trust us as politicians. They can no longer accept the political lies delivered over the past 14 years by this Government.
We come now to 1978-79. We had another Minister of Finance, the Hon. Jean Chretien, who followed the Hon. Donald Macdonald. In his budget address of November 16, 1978, he said:
There can be no weakening in our determination to keep expenditures under tight control.
By that time, Mr. Speaker, spending on a national accounts basis was at $43.9 billion, the deficit was $12.2 billion and the net debt was $44.9 billion. Again we see the evolution of political rhetoric in a direction exactly opposite to that of the reality of extravagance and irresponsible management of the public tax resource.
On January 12, 1980, the Prime Minister said: "We will hold the line of Government expenditure growth to under the rate of the Gross National Product". That was the first time we heard about this extravagant spending being now related to Gross National Product. He told the nation: "The deficit will be reduced in a phased and orderly fashion. Any new expenditure programs to meet evolving needs and requirements of Canadians will be financed by reallocating existing expenditures or by increases in revenues. We will not add to the deficit by adding new programs." At that time spending on a national accounts basis was at $54.4 billion, the annual deficit was $11.48 billion, going down slightly through the year of Mr. Chretien, and the net debt was $57 billion.
In Mr. MacEachen's period, spending rose to $89.5 billion when he was finally tossed out. The annual debt doubled from $12.6 billion to $25.25 billion and the net debt rose from $68.5 billion to $95 billion. Mr. MacEachen was the man who belittled the previous Minister of Finance in the Clark Government, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). He belittled him time after time in the House by saying he would never bring down a budget that would put 18 cents a gallon tax on gasoline. In this period of time there was the other massive mistruth or lie and 18 cents a gallon soon became 18 cents a litre under the next Government. Eighteen cents a gallon became 77 cents a gallon after belittling 18 cents.
It comes down to 15 years of rhetoric, Mr. Speaker, all of it misleading. The Liberal Government has known all through the last decade and a half the consequences of profligate spending and management of the federal tax resource. One can legitimately conclude that its attack on the free enterprise

market economy has been deliberate. It has said one thing in support of it, it has espoused the rules of management which you need to espouse to remain healthy as a nation, and it has done exactly the opposite. The Government knew that if the nation continued to pay ourselves more than the value of what we produced we would create the high unemployment that we have today. Any thinking, average educated person knew that that was coming.
Did this so-called Liberal Government spend money advocating the need to reduce our anticipation levels? No, sir, they did not. That was probably the one thing we had to do above all others. We had to reduce the anticipation level of the nation as we came out of a period of affluence. Did the Government spend money advocating the need to improve our productivity? I do not remember seeing any advertisements in that regard. 1 heard a lot of talk in the House about the fact that if we did not improve our productivity we would not be able to reduce inflation. The Prime Minister used to tell us that time and time again. Instead of doing just those two things with the information through the advertising dollars that it had the power to spend, what did it do? The Government launched into an extravaganza of telling us the virtues of nationalization and the virtues of VIA Rail, that Crown corporation which has to draw $50 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for every ticket it sells. There is no bottom line management there at all. They have put full and half page ads in the paper extolling the virtues of Canadair. Canadair is the Crown corporation which just had to write off $ 1.4 billion.

on Crown employees and other sectors of the nation. During that period when everyone else was to hunker down in order to reduce the effects of inflation on our lives and our country, the Government went ahead with the most lavish and outlandish expenditure on advertising, advocacy and information that one could imagine.
During the six and five period in the last two years, according to information taken directly from the Supplementary Estimates (B), the Economic Development Department moved its advertising expenditure from $2,000 through to $575,000. That is a 28,000 per cent increase. The budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans for advertising and advocacy went from $1.5 million to $4 million. That is a 161 per cent increase. There was a 35 per cent increase in this area for the Department of National Revenue. Why does that Department not tell the people of Canada that it now goes straight into their bank accounts without giving them the courtesy of a notice? Why has it not spent money on advertising that or advertising changes in interpretation bulletins and other matters? Instead, it does so by stealth. It will go into bank accounts before it tells owners.
For Science and Technology, the increase was 558 per cent. That sounds like a large increase, but the budget only moved from $73,000 to $481,000 although this is the most important area of our lives in Canada today. But Science and Technology has absolutely no priority at all.
The advertising and information budget for the Department of the Environment increased by 50 per cent. The increase for Communications was 126 per cent and Justice had an increase of 666 per cent. This all occurred during the six and five era. So much for saying one thing and doing another.
When one considers the Main Estimates and the Supplementary Estimates, there has been an increase in spending of 14 per cent through this six and five period. On August 13, 1969 the Prime Minister said:
We could not tolerate a 14 per cent increase in federal expenditures. If allowed to grow unchecked, eventually- our spending would become so scattered that the real needs of our society would be missed.
That is what he said. He continued:
And to spend vast sums on welfare, education and other programs while allowing inflation to continue would merely place hundreds of thousands of Canadians on a treadmill from which they could not escape.
We are on that treadmill today. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is in the House. She is in a struggle with some Provinces that are on this treadmill and do not know how to budget their affairs. That is what the Government has delivered as a result of saying one thing and doing exactly the opposite.
In March, 1976 the Auditor General's Report warned that if the Government continued to spend at its current rate, the nation would be out of control. He told us that it was out of control and spoke of the critically serious situation we faced in this country. But nothing has happened since that warning. The Government has continued its reckless spending and slothful, wasteful habits. We have not addressed old programs as the Prime Minister said we should. The old programs have just become a base upon which incremental increases are added.
It is obvious that between the bureaucracy and those elected to govern nothing will happen in this area unless it takes place in the House. The House has put a group of 20 of its Members to work in the Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure and the reorganization of rules in the House. Those of us on that Committee saw a need to move the influence of the House back into a stronger position over the habits of the bureaucracy and Governments in power. This problem will not be addressed until the House addresses it and until elected Members within it undertake the responsibility and recognize the seriousness of the extravaganza of the last 14 years to begin to bring it back under control.
We are dealing with human nature and the House is full of that emotion. However, I say that if we do not begin now to apply ourselves to a corrective pattern over the slothful extravagance of expenditure, we are doing a total disservice to our children and those who follow. We are threatening the survival of this democratic system and we are putting their freedom on the platter.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the motion before us presented by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) is quoted a remark made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1969. Contrary to what is implied in the motion, this Government has in fact since that date implemented a whole range of policies to improve the management and control of its expenditures.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
I want to give some concrete examples of this. For that purpose, I want to discuss first the Government's policy on its spending. The Government's white paper of October 14, 1975, contained the following statement of policy:
The federal Government shares the view that the trend of total spending by all Governments should not rise more quickly than the trend of the Gross National Product.
Supply
Ceilings on total outlays in the ensuing years have been established in general accordance with this statement. The record of expenditures itself reflects the general success of the Government in holding the growth rate of total outlays below the rate of growth of the Gross National Product. Although the recession has understandably resulted in expenditure growth in excess of Gross National Product growth for the last two years, this principle outlined in 1975 continues to govern the determination of our over-all, multi-year expenditure plan. Of course, as I have said, the Government's expenditures in the past two years have gone up to offset the effects of the recent recession by providing further resources for direct job-creation, supporting investment by the private sector, the Government's own Special Recovery Projects, and more support for housing, all to create more jobs as well as protecting the unemployed through more expenditures on programs like unemployment insurance.
Last April the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) confirmed the commitment of the Government to the principle that the growth rate of total outlays should be in line with the rate of growth of the Gross National Product. He said:
This commitment was met until the recession last year. I am reaffirming this commitment tonight. The fiscal plan 1 will be tabling with this budget shows that total outlays as a share of GNP will fall steadily from this year to 1986-1987. By that year, federal spending will be virtually the same size relative to the economy as in 1981-1982, before the worst of the recession. To achieve this outcome will demand continuing diligence in restraining expenditure growth.
One year after the announcement in 1975 of its policy on over-all expenditures, the Government further made manifest its intent to improve the management and control of its expenditures, and of Government more broadly, for that matter, by establishing the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability, the Lambert Commission.
The terms of reference by the Commission as set out by the Government clearly reflect its concerns. These terms referred to unprecedented demands placed on government by the growth requested by the public in its responsibilities and programs, a desire to ensure efficiency and probity in the Public Service of Canada, a serious concern about the adequacy of financial administration in government for establishing effective control over, and accountability for, public funds, and the need to use resources effectively, avoid waste and increase productivity in Government.
Even before the Commission began its deliberations and up until the present, the Government has been taking a range of steps to respond to these concerns and thereby strengthen management and accountability throughout Government. I would like at this time to touch briefly on some of the major initiatives in the last six or seven years.
In conjunction with, and in support of, the general policy to hold spending generally in line with the rate of growth of the GNP, the growth in the size of the Public Service has been tightly constrained. Growth in person-years under Treasury Board control has been explicitly limited as a matter of policy to no more than 1 per cent annually in the last several years and, despite heavy pressures on government programs, the size

November 28, 1983
Supply
of the Public Service under Treasury Board control is almost the same today as it was in 1976-1977.
There has been the introduction of the Policy and Expenditure Management System, the envelope system. This was another major step forward. It provides an expenditure management framework that sets multi-year levels for both total outlays and for various envelopes or policy sectors. It establishes policy committees within cabinet to undertake policy development and decision making within the discipline of the envelope system. While the previous Conservative Government introduced key portions of this system, the current Government has provided its consolidation and final implementation.
I would also remind Hon. Members that the key developmental work on the envelope system was undertaken before the previous Conservative Government was in office.
A key elaboration of PEMS, another way of describing the envelope system, has been the introduction by the Treasury Board of the Multi-year Operational Planning System. This system is aimed at fostering more integrated resource planning, budgeting and management throughout the Government. Two key concepts, budgeting to results and budgeting for management, underlie the Multi-Year Operational Plans submitted to the Treasury Board. The first concept is designed to facilitate practical but systematic budgetary analysis based on concrete program outputs and inputs. The second is aimed at providing a clear understanding throughout the Government of the responsibilities of Public Service managers and how these responsibilities translate into budgetary requirements.
The office of the Comptroller General, created in 1978 in response to a central recommendation of the Lambert Commission, assists in the establishment of sound management practices in the federal Government by developing policies and standards and by promoting and monitoring improvements in financial and operational management. Over the last four years 30 or so key departments have participated in one of the Comptroller General's key initiatives called Improvement in Management Practices and Controls, or IMPAC, which is directed at the internal management process of individual departments. IMPAC has resulted in the establishment of action plans for over 100 major projects to improve organization, planning, internal and external reporting, automation, program delivery procedures, audit and program evaluation. Almost 80 per cent of the work on these projects has now been completed, and there is clear evidence of the ongoing yields that are the result. The IMPAC program has identified a total of more than $250 million in annual recurring benefits, of which more than $122 million in annual recurring savings have already been realized.
Substantial progress has been made in implementing the revised form of the Estimates, extending significantly the information made available to Parliament. The Government now presents in the form of Part I a summary of its spending plans in straightforward language and numbers. I am sure the Hon. Member for Capilano will recall his own role with respect to the creation of this document. In the Part III volumes detailed information is being made available on the
individual programs in each Department and agency with the express intention of improving the accountability to Parliament by the Government. All of these major initiatives, along with numerous others, have been in the spirit of the recommendations of the Lambert Commission and have contributed to a new framework for management in the Public Service, one which is comprehensive and coherent, yet is also flexible and adaptable and which facilitates accountability.
I would now like to say something about the nature of the Government's current expenditure plan, using it to illustrate the key forces at play in trying to maintain over-all expenditures roughly constant in relation to GNP over the longer term, while responding as effectively and as efficiently as possible to the very real needs of the people of this country.
First, I would like to review briefly the important role in total spending played by statutory expenditure items and other programs providing automatic stabilizers designed to offer Canadians some measure of social and economic shelter in turbulent economic times. Second, I want to comment on that relatively small portion of total spending attributable to the operating costs of all Government Departments.
As the Minister of Finance has indicated, the worst of the very difficult economic climate is behind us. Canadians are regaining their confidence, growth is resuming, inflation is down dramatically, as are interest rates. Unemployment has also decreased but remains distressingly high. Job creation, therefore, continues to be a major Government priority.
The 1983-84 expenditure plan calls for total spending of $90.7 billion, an increase of 12.7 per cent or $10.2 billion over 1982-83. Of this increase, a little over $1 billion is attributable to the rise in public debt charges, almost $1 billion to increased defence costs and over $1.5 billion is directly due to new spending initiatives announced in the budget, including over $500 million for the Special Recovery Capital Projects which are aimed at encouraging and facilitating economic recovery in Canada.
Of the remaining spending increase of about $6.8 billion spread over hundreds of Government activities, fully one-half is entirely due to increases in only four major programs Government contributions to unemployment insurance, the Old Age Security, the guaranteed income supplement and spouse's allowances programs, and payments to the Provinces under the Established Programs Financing, that is to say, post-secondary education, medicare and the Canada Assistance Plan.
These programs are, of course, the core of our social and economic security system. They provide enhanced and extended benefits to the unemployed throughout Canada, particularly in the regions hardest hit by the recession. They offer basic income support to the aged, particularly those with lower incomes. They support the financing of at least 50 per cent of the cost of hospital insurance, medicare, extended health care, post-secondary education and social assistance payments, welfare services, child support services such as foster care and
November 28, 1983

daycare, and a broad range of other family and social support services.
I have highlighted these large elements in our expenditure plan because of the special importance such programs take on the tough economic times as automatic stabilizers against some of the worst effects of a recession and the gradual, fragile recovery period we have just entered.
I do not think we should overestimate the scope for changing some of our most basic programs since what Government does reflects society's views of its goals and how Government can assist in achieving them. We must, after all, face some fairly definite facts. For example, there are historic costs associated with the attainment of interprovincial and inter-regional equity in Canada. There are also the costs of achieving a standard of interpersonal equity in Canada.
Successive generations have shared a view of social equity and have succeeded in having it reflected in laws which for many people are tantamount to being the social as well as the legal definition of what it means to be Canadian. While we may consider changing some of those laws, I doubt that Canadians would want us to put at risk fundamental values and goals in pursuit of arbitrary approaches to limiting Government spending.
Of course, in what I have said 1 have not intended to imply that there is no room at all for streamlining and repriorizing federal activities, and consequently spending, while still effectively meeting the demands on Government posed in a changing environment. 1 believe we have demonstrated the ability, through processes like the envelope system, to make increasingly tough decisions about programs and policy trade-offs. For example, in his economic statement in the House of Commons last fall, the Minister of Finance cited the reallocation of $1.1 billion from existing programs to new ones, primarily to stimulate job creation at a time of unacceptably high levels of unemployment. However, 1 must add that this reallocation did not reflect a judgment that this money was being wasted in its previous application, but rather a judgment of priorities.
In the crucible of difficult economic times, it is a transfer of Government support from some very worthy purposes to others which are currently more urgent. However, as I have pointed out, and as I will illustrate further in a few minutes, the room we have to do this, without making fundamental changes in the transfer programs for which the largest portion of federal expenditures are made, is much more limited than most people realize.
One of the major challenges to all Canadians is the need to improve the productivity and competitiveness of our economy. Of course, achieving productivity gains across all sectors of the national economy is beyond the single-handed ability of the federal Government. It requires a co-operative and joint effort by business, labour and Government-in short, by all Canadians.
However, there are ways in which the Government can act and is acting concurrently and supportively. One way is to

demonstrate that we intend to and can enhance the productivity of the Government's own operations. As I indicated when I tabled the current year's Main Estimates, as President of the Treasury Board I have set as a major priority continuing this Government's policy of improving the federal Government's management and the efficiency and effectiveness of its programs.
Perhaps I should clarify my definitions of efficiency and effectiveness in Government. Efficiency refers to the way we manage our resources in order to minimize the cost of delivery of Government programs. Effectiveness, on the other hand, refers to the range and the quality of the services that Government delivers to the Canadian people, as well as the extent to which these services meet the objectives expected of them.
As we seek to improve the efficiency of Government as I have defined this concept, it is important to understand the scale of the Government costs involved, since one frequently has the impression of a misinformed, exaggerated view on the part of some that somehow the bulk of the $90 billion federal budget is being squandered on Public Service salaries and perks. The truth of the matter is, of course, that about three-quarters, or about $68 billion of the $90 billion, consists of payments we make to Provinces, businesses, groups and individuals in Canada, as well as for external aid purposes, and from which the recipients benefit directly. The actual cost of developing, administering and delivering these programs is of the order of $12 billion for all Departments and agencies, leaving aside the $8 billion for national defence and the $2 billion for capital projects. Of this $12 billion, about $8 billion is for wages, salaries and employee benefits.
Therefore, while I am confident the federal Government can demonstrate commitment to obtaining efficiencies in administration, I must stress that any such administrative savings obviously will not produce any drastic reductions in the deficit, nor in the size and role of government.
When every Canadian shares a role with every other Canadian in making our national economy more competitively productive, it becomes important for government administration to establish and maintain a high standard of efficient and effective operations. The Government has in the recent past taken a number of steps further to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of its operations, initiatives such as IMPAC and the multi-year operational planning process that I have already mentioned.
These kinds of initiatives seek to compensate for the multiple goals often found in the public sector and the lack of an automatic, profit-based bottom line as is available in the private sector, by emphasizing the need for a formal and clear definition and articulation of the results which each program of the Government is expected to achieve. They also involve the development of systems and procedures to allow for measurement of the extent to which the results promised are in fact realized.

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, 1 disagree with my hon. friend's contention that we have ignored the Auditor General's Reports. He spoke as well of sensing a new attitude with respect to improved financial control and so on. I do not think we have been ignoring the Auditor General's Reports. In fact, one of the main jobs of the Comptroller General, through programs Like IMPAC, is to develop definitions for improved productivity within the Public Service and to develop programs to carry out these definitions.
1 repeat what I said in my remarks to the House a few months ago. Unlike the private sector, there is no simple and automatic bottom line definition of productivity or of the results we are seeking within the Government. The Government has a multiplicity of goals, often goals which the private sector could not and would not work toward when applying a strictly profit-based bottom line. This is one of the challenges faced by the Government in terms of over-all improvement of its productivity. That does not mean we should not try to improve productivity.
We are moving in the direction of improved productivity and are making progress through programs like the IMPAC program of the Auditor General. This can be confirmed by the fact that the programs put in place through IMPAC have already demonstrated annual savings of $122 million. These savings are not simply one-time savings but annual savings, with more savings expected as other programs are in place. This shows that we are taking seriously the recommendations of people like the Auditor General.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank you very much for recognizing me at this point. The debate before us concerns the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in a televised press conference, and I want to read his quotation into the record again: "We'd soon be on the road to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control". We are on the road to financial disaster because nothing was done to bring spending under control. That is exactly the point of this debate. It disturbs me that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), who was here earlier, is not here to follow the debate further through the day.
We have a tremendous country. In our country we have relatively young, educated people. The possibility of resources in our soils and water are unparalleled anywhere in the world. There is really no reason we should be in the difficulty we are in. For every dollar the Government spends this year, over 30 cents will have to be either borrowed or printed. That certainly puts us well down the road to disaster.
Until 1975 we had deficits but they were not of the order, magnitude or percentage of Gross National Product of the deficits we have had since that time. Mr. John Turner, the then Minister of Finance, started the program of spending

November 28, 1983
Supply
much more than was conceivably taken in taxes. Every year since he was Minister of Finance our deficit position has become worse and worse. It is on that particular problem that 1 would like to address the House today.
In the past year, despite what the President of the Treasury Board said earlier, the percentage of the Gross National Product used directly by the Government rose to 47.3 per cent in 1982. That did not take into account the tremendous amounts of money controlled and spent by Crown corporations in supplying services and engaging in activities, some of which are profitable and some of which are very unprofitable. Therefore, the amount of the Gross National Product that is controlled by the Government has now reached the point where over half of what is created and developed in this country is done by the Government. That has led to the mess we are in.
Let me refer to some of the facts and figures that were set out by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on April 19. Even if we take into account the exceeding optimism expressed by the Minister in his budget statement, I point out that we have now arrived at a position where our deficits will not allow the country to break even. Even under the most optimistic conditions, such as having virtually 100 per cent employment and the country proceeding at full speed, we would still have a deficit of approximately 3.5 per cent of the Gross National Product.
I say this with regard to the Government's statement which was filed on April 19 and Members are at liberty to look at that documentation. Members will recall that there was a special presentation on the effect of deficits contained within the budget papers. The evidence, as clearly stated by the Department of Finance in its presentation to the House, was that we have that kind of a structural deficit.
The House will recall that the Government's projections in its Fiscal plan indicated that we would have a very good year next year when there would be an increase in the Gross National Product of the country of 5.2 per cent. That would be followed in 1985-86 with an increase of 4.4 per cent and the same thing the following year, 1986-87. However, if we follow this deficit position of the Government during those years, even with this enormous growth rate which 1 point out is far in excess of what we experienced in the 1970s, the Government deficit would still be in excess of $25 billion. Its borrowing requirements would be in excess of $19 billion. The result is that even with projected good times, boom times, if you like, the Government will not come close to balancing the books of the country. This must change.
This country, no more than any individual who runs a household, cannot use credit year after year to pay the grocery bill. We must eventually have a balance. It has never been required that government should be able to balance its books every year. During tough times such as we have experienced in the last two years, perhaps governments should be allowed to go into a deficit position. That is what is called a cyclical deficit. In good times the Government should show a surplus.
But I would point out that the Government's present actions make it impossible ever to show a surplus. Indeed, a deficit is built right into the system and, according to the Estimates filed in the House by the Minister of Finance on April 19, the deficit is close to 3.5 per cent of the GNP.
This means that at the present time the Government would either have to increase taxes by approximately $14 billion or $15 billion, reduce its expenditures by the same amount, or perhaps a combination of both.
Let us look at the question of increasing taxes. I think we are all aware that there are precious little opportunities available for large tax increases in the country. Canadians are already paying a level of tax that is in excess of the tax level paid by our trading partner, the United States.
As a practical matter, it is impossible for one nation to have a tax impost that is higher than that of its competitor and trading partner. While there could be different taxes within each country, the over-all effect of taxation must be approximately the same or the country with the higher taxation level will suffer dramatically. Indeed, that is what is happening in Canada today.
Generally speaking, taxes in the United States are considerably lower than those in Canada. That is one of the major reasons the United States did not go as deeply into the recession as Canada and is coming out of it much more rapidly and dramatically than we are. That is why over-all employment in the United States is one million more than it was before the recession, and why over-all employment in Canada is 250,000 less than it was when we went into the recession. Therefore I see no way that we can dramatically increase taxes to cover that structural deficit.
Let us look at the other alternative, that is, to cut our suit to meet the amount of cloth available. This requires some prioriz-ing of Government expenditures. We must consider what the country should do to get itself back on a sound footing. First, 1 believe we should begin with the concept of zero-based budgeting. I do not believe that Government Departments such as the Department of Agriculture for example, can continue to have its budget automatically increased to meet inflation. This should apply to all Government Departments. With respect to programs, I believe we must get down to the brass tacks of coldly and calculatingly deciding which programs we must keep and which ones we must discard. Interestingly enough, I was reading to Prime Minister's statement which was referred to in the motion and that is what he said in 1968. That is not what he did but what he said.
Next, we should consider carrying out the recommendations suggested by what is commonly referred to as the Huntington-Lachance report. Specifically, this deals with the question of priorizing expenditures and involving the House in that process. In other words, we should create an estimates committee of the House that will work with the Treasury Board in priorizing and determining the expenditures of the Government and where that money should be allocated. It is my view, and I believe that of my Party, that the first obligation of
November 28, 1983

government is to ensure that the social service network which is in place is maintained.

Mr. Speaker, last week on Private Members' day the Government talked out a Private Member's Bill on maintenance. This was a Bill directed to simplifying maintenance orders. It had the defects of a Private Member's Bill, and it is not the solution to the problem we need. Nevertheless, it is time to ask the Government what it is doing to bring in legislation on the matter.
The appalling rates of non-payment of maintenance orders have been known for years. The Law Reform Commission back in 1969 made recommendations for a more effective system. These were endorsed, and other recommendations were made by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada in 1970. Yet in 1976 another Law Reform Commission study reported that most maintenance payments were in arrears to some extent. The Government is on very poor grounds now in November, 1983, to be saying that more time is needed to study the complexities of the matter.
Thousands of Canadian women and children live in poverty as a result of nonpayment of maintenance orders. Last June the federal-provincial Committee on Enforcement of Maintenance and Custody Orders reported, with a number of specific and concrete recommendations for reform. Some require federal action, or joint federal-provincial action. Federal legislation is needed to facilitate the location of the defaulters and to make maintenance orders binding on pension benefits, estates, unemployment insurance benefits, and income tax refunds. The object is prompt, automatic enforcement.
A unified family court system is needed to permit one-step access to maintenance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has taken some recent initiatives to boost Canada's steel industries. The changes to the Crow rate and the expansion of the rail networks in western Canada will give Canadian steel companies a chance to bid competitively for millions of dollars in contracts. As well, the Anti-Dumping Tribunal is currently looking into several claims put forth by Canadian steel companies about unfair pricing on some steel imports. However, it is a very serious concern to me that the Government of the Province of Ontario is presently considering ending the steel industry's monopoly on soft drink can production.
Stelco and Dofasco have carried out a department by department analysis of the impact on employment of the loss of the soft drink can market. Their analysis has shown that such a ruling would result in a loss of 607 jobs, with 560 of those lost jobs being in Hamilton and Nanticoke. Although these job figures are for the soft drink can market for all of Canada, a loss of the Ontario market would make production for the rest of Canada uneconomic.
The current regulations state that 85 per cent of each soft drink can must be made of steel. In light of the hardships that the steel industry has recently endured, a decision to end its monopoly in soft drink can production would be extremely burdensome. 1 therefore sincerely recommend that the Ontario Cabinet protect the steel industry's jobs in these difficult times.

Mr. Speaker, when we broke at lunch I was going over some of the priorities that I felt a House of Commons committee might look at in determining the priorizing of government expenditures. I was speaking about social services.
From this Party's point of view, we would expect that the first priority of any government expenditure would be to make sure that those less fortunate in our society had some of the opportunities, protections and safeguards in terms of education and health that those more fortunate have. Unfortunately, in some of our social service expenditures there is a tendency to look after the greedy more than the needy. In looking at those expenditures one might want to do some screening to determine whether those expenditures are really for those who need the service as opposed to those who happen to want to get to the trough. Basically, our view would be that the social net, the ability to look after our neighbours, is a thing that we look to government for first. Expenditures on social services would be our first priority.
Our second priority would go to the question of defending our nation. We think it is terrible that we do not spend sufficient money to protect our nation but rather depend, to some extent, on the nuclear arm of the United States for our protection. If we are going to have a place in the world and be respected in the world, and if we are going to protect our heritage, then surely we must spend more of our country's wealth in looking after that heritage.
The third point is that people in Canada demand that we use our funds to look after the sense of justice that is required; that the criminal law be enforced, that we have police protection to protect us from those in our society who might want to take advantage of us and that there be a fairness in the administration of justice. That that would be a priority.
Next, there would be a priority in terms of communication and transportation. After all, we are a great, diverse nation and we must keep our nation together. Therefore, expenditures in terms of communication and transportation are important expenditures which deserve some priority.

After you go beyond those you look at the other things that government does and you find that to a large extent what government does is spend money, but not very well. I have not been in this House that long, but 1 have heard Minister after Minister stand in the House and tell us how many jobs his Department or his program was creating. Indeed, if the Government has created all the jobs it has created, everyone in Canada would be working at least three shifts a day, seven days a week, trying to fulfil those jobs. The fact is that the Government is not very efficient at creating jobs. It is the private sector which creates jobs, the people with ideas and entrepreurial ability who create jobs. It is a waste of Government funds for the Government to try to do something which it does not do well.
We should consider what the Government can do. I have suggested some of those possibilities. The Government cannot entertain us well. The Government, through CBC and other activities which it tries to encourage in the name of culture, spends a lot of money trying to entertain us. The basic question is whether it is doing it very well. I suggest that any committee which would look into that would see those expenditures with a somewhat jaundiced eye.
The third point is that governments are in competition with each other. As a result, we see provincial Governments in this country with trade embassies in London, Paris and Rome. As well federal Governments have trade embassies in the same places. That duplication, and triplication in some instances with respect to health services, must be eliminated. Surely we could have a mechanism to determine which government may be best suited to do a job that is required. There would be no need for the involvement of other governments.
For instance, with respect to the health and medicare proposals made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), perhaps we should bear in mind where the responsibilities lie. If it is a provincial responsibility, perhaps the provincial Governments should deal with that responsibility and relieve the federal Government of the responsibility so it will not spend money from the federal treasury on those activities.
That is not to say that there should not be transfers of tax money from one jurisdiction to another. It does not mean that there should not be transfers to make sure there is equal opportunity in Canada. But the federal Government should not be involved in activities that clearly fall within provincial responsibility. It is a waste of money and effort. It is something which significantly increases our deficit.
Having determined what envelopes are available and how they are established, we should get down to the basic matter of how much money can properly be taken out of the system in terms of taxation. When that is determined, we ought to limit the spending of the Government to that amount while maintaining a healthy economy.
I appreciate that changes cannot be made instantly. We already have a system which has saddled us with what
amounts to a deficit of some $30 billion. The Government's priorities cannot be changed overnight in order to get us back into a position where government will balance on a cyclical basis. That must be our objective and one which a new government must attempt over a five or six year period. It may even take longer than that since the present Government has put us into a horrendously difficult financial position. We cannot easily wean ourselves from that difficulty. To some extent, we are almost like heroin addicts. We have been given a shot of more money in government services every year than we can afford to pay for and it will take us some time to withdraw from that level of government spending to which we have unfortunately become accustomed. It certainly is a level that we cannot afford. It will take a new government a number of years to get our country back into the position in which it should have been had the present Government followed its own leader's advice.
In order to reach that goal I believe it is necessary to follow the recommendation of the report by the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure to create a special committee of the House to priorize government expenditures and act as a supervisory committee over how parliamentarians authorize the expenditures of taxpayers' money. That is the beginning of a long litany of sins committed in his speech. It seems to me that when one puts forward an amendment, one should understand what the amendment is supposed to do with regard to the main motion.
We heard today from the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the Hon. Member for Mississauga South a litany of comments from history to the effect that great problems have occurred in this country as a result of deficits, as though there was some insidious plot to nationalize the entire economy, and so on and so forth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We should take this whole question of deficits into perspective. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South did speak about what he called a structural deficit and a cyclical deficit. I think we have to understand, and the people certainly understand, that we have just gone through the most massive recession worldwide that has occurred in the past 50 years. This Government did not want to impose or see imposed upon
its people the kind of suffering that occurred in the 1930s. In talking to my senior citizens, I asked them what happened in the 1930s and whether they could compare the current recession with the 1930s. They told me there is no comparison. There is no comparison because we put in place a highly sophisticated, highly effective social safety net that has protected Canadians in a way that was simply unknown and unhoped for in the 1930s. There is no doubt about that, Mr. Speaker. We have protected Canadians who were struck by unemployment. We have protected Canadians who were unable to work because they were senior citizens and because they were infirm. That social safety net is there. It is strong. It is doing the job it is supposed to do. However, it costs money. I am asking the Opposition Members during this debate to stand in their place and say that the deficit is more important than the social and financial security of Canadians. If I hear that, I will know where the Conservatives stand. I do not know where they stand now.
We hear the great rail about the terrible deficit, "Oh my God, the deficit has to be brought down immediately." In another part of my speech I will bring forward statements by Members opposite, Members who out of one side of their mouth cry for a reduction in the deficit and out of the other side cry for increased expenditures in their own riding. You cannot have it both ways. Either you believe in reducing the deficit at all costs, or you do not. You cannot stand up one day and say the deficit is too high, that it has to be reduced and there has to be greater fiscal responsibility in this country and the next day stand up in the House and say that the Government must spend billions more on job creation, billions more on research and development, billions more on national defence, billions more on forestry and billions more for fisheries. You have to come down on the issue. Either you believe in it or you do not.
The clear, unequivocal answer to that question is that the Tories do not really believe it. They are putting up the deficit and pulling scare tactics on the Canadian people. However, when it comes right down to the bottom line, the Tories will not be dealing with that deficit. To do so, they would have to attack programs that Canadians have come to hold dearly, programs that have supported Canadians well during the worst recession the world has known in 50 years. That is the bottom line. It is a bottom line to which these Tories will not respond.
We have heard that Canadian Governments in general, but the federal Government in particular, have allowed the deficit to run away, almost as though it had accelerated continuously during the 1970s. The facts are here. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) was talking about the total government sector. With regard to the total Government sector, the deficit in Canada as a percentage of GNP peaked in 1978. It declined steadily until 1981. In 1982-83, we went into a recession. If the automatic stabilizers have any meaning at all, it would imply that when you go into a recession and the revenues of the government fall, people are thrown out of work, social expenditures rise, the deficit as a percentage of

GNP is going to rise. Precisely that effect is what is intended. When the economy is crumbling, the social safety net takes up the slack, substitutes income to people so that they are not thrown out on the street in destitution. That is what the safety social net is all about.
Yes, the deficit as a percentage of GNP rose during the recession. Thank God it did. If it had not, people would have been thrown out on the street. They would have lost their homes by the thousands. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) is going to rise in great indignation, but the point is that the deficit peaked in 1978, declined steadily until 1981 and then rose again.
Let us look at some comparisons. We heard a lot about comparisons, how Canadian Governments had run-away deficits unknown in any other part of the world. Let me quote some figures. In the period 1975-1981, the Canadian deficit averaged 2.1 per cent of GNP. In the United States it was 1.3 per cent, in Britain 3.7 per cent, in Germany 3.4 per cent, in Italy 9.7 per cent and in Japan 4.1 per cent, compared to 2.1 per cent of GNP in the Canadian deficit average.
During that period, the Canadian deficit was declining. We all admit that it rose during the recession, but there is not one Member opposite who has the intestinal fortitude to talk to his or her constituents or any other constituents in this country and say that he does not think the deficit should have risen during the recession and then tell Canadians how he would have stopped it from rising. When the world goes into a recession, being a trading nation, we are going to be affected by that. There is no doubt about it. That is clear, straightforward fact.

By not creating unemployment in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, when we are talking about a near doubling on defence, which would go from 2 per cent of Gross National Product to 3.5 per cent of Gross National Product, that is not primarily an increase in manpower although one Hon. Member spoke about an increase in our NATO equipment back to 10,000.

The Hon. Member has raised other issues. According to what he has said in the past, I believe he is seriously concerned about the size of the deficit. I am concerned about it and 1 am concerned about the size of the interest payments because that is money that is not being spent to provide good social services and other goods to Canadians.
We have gone through a period of very high interest rates but we have been able to bring down the world economy and we have contributed to bringing interest rates down substantially. As those bonds are refinanced, the interest cost of the debt is going to be reduced. If we can keep inflation down, and I think we can, interest rates will come down further and the interest cost of the debt will be reduced.
If we can get growth going and the deficit is reduced as a percentage of the Gross National Product, then we will be in a position where the interest expense and the size of the deficit will be manageable. The nub of the issue today is whether, during a period of serious recession, the Government should be condemned for doing what a Government with a strong social conscience should do, and that is, protect the people who need protection the most. speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with utter amazement and some despair to the Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans). 1 do not know where he has been this last while. Perhaps, being isolated in Ottawa, he does not understand the suffering and the problems that have been created in the country for the millions of people who are unemployed. He passed that off as if there really were no problem for them. If he had seen the reports in the weekend newspapers, he would know what one organization after the other is saying is the terrible social cost borne by millions of Canadians as a result of the policies of the Government. Canadians are being thrown into despair, anxiety and anguish because of steps which his colleagues took which he backed up. I do not know where he has been when he stands up and makes statements like he does.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What policies?

He should take a look at headlines in the papers which say what the Government has been doing over this last few years. "Lives of millions in jeopardy" reads the weekend edition of the Kingston Whig-Standard. From the Ottawa Citizen we have "Unemployment destroying lives".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Tell us how the Government caused that.

From the Saturday Toronto Star we have "Jobless rate spells ruin, group warns." The Canadian Mental Health Association, the Family Services Association, both say it was the unemployment policies of this Government which have thrown those people into the despair they are in today. They are afraid to listen to the truth; that is what is wrong with Members opposite. Every time Canadians try to bring home the difficulties they are in, those Members get up and run.
The motion before us today, Mr. Speaker, addresses the financial disaster precipitated by Members of this Government-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Name them.

These policies have led not only to financial disaster, Sir, but also to human suffering and misery for millions of Canadians. The policies of this Government have led to widespread lay-offs, falling incomes, a decline in productivity and sharply reduced employment opportunities for many hundreds of young people. The failure of the Government to recognize the impact of its sterile economic policies has, in turn, generated massive social costs which could have been averted if proper economic policies had been adopted.
There are a number of direct ways by which we can calculate the tremendous and escalating costs of the doubledigit unemployment which, over the past two years, unfortunately, has become the norm for Canada. We can look at the cost of unemployment insurance benefits, which will total $11 billion this year. Two years ago that cost was $5 billion. We can look at the revenues of the federal Government, which are down 3 per cent so far this fiscal year from two years ago. We can look at the 1.4 million Canadians officially counted as unemployed and looking for work. We can look at the 100,000 Canadians who have given up looking for work, and the
400,000	trying to make it with part-time jobs when they want to get full-time jobs. These are the direct costs, Mr. Speaker, and they are staggering. They come out of the 1981 budget of the former Minister of Finance, the National Energy Program and a whole host of other programs which this Government foisted on this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Nonsense. Where have you been?

Those are the direct costs. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that while you can put more or less

realistic dollar figures on them, there are other more frightening costs which are all too often ignored.

Mr. Speaker, I am talking about the social suffering resulting from the unemployment, the despair of people who have lost their jobs and their homes, young people who have never been able to find regular employment. Add to this the state of hopelessness and utter despair that leads to family break-up, violence, increases in crime, and mental and physical sickness. These costs are rarely calculated. In fact, it is probably impossible to do so, but they are there just the same. Who can put a figure on the cost to a family, to a son, daughter, husband and wife who have been looking for employment for weeks or even months without success and where the situation has become almost intolerable? Last week, the press reported that according to a Gallup poll, three out of ten Canadians, which means 30 per cent of the people of this country, are still suffering from the pain associated with unemployment. [English]
In case there is any doubt, Mr. Speaker, as to the connection between unemployment and the agony and cost to a family, let me refer to two major reports which were released in the past week. The first is by the Association of Family Service Agencies and it was released in both Canada and the United States. That Association said that unemployment has become the greatest threat to family stability in Canada and the United States in the past two years. It goes on to cite the tremendous social costs which will have to be borne as a result.
The Canadian Mental Health Association over the past weekend cited the direct links between unemployment and the disastrous consequences to Canadian family life. It said that family life in Canada is becoming filled with anger and despair, and child abuse, suicide, alcoholism, disease, divorce and crime are soaring as a result of unemployment. That unemployment was triggered by this Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Nonsense.

Earlier this year. Sir, the officials of the Ministry of State for Economic and Regional Development had the courage to own up to what was taking place. They knew where the responsibility lay for this. They produced a paper which showed this. They frankly conceded that policy-induced high interest rates were one of the major causes of the recession here in Canada and explained why it has been deeper in this country than in any other industrialized country. Policy-induced high interest rates, the Minister's own advisers have said, have led us to the depths of this depression. Yet the Government abdicates responsibility for the recession, while at the same time, if there is any hint of recovery, it goes out and says, "Look, we are responsible for that." That is the double standard which Government continually foists on both the economy and the people of Canada.
Hon. Members opposite, Mr. Speaker, want Canadians to develop amnesia, to accept the current situation as normal, to forget that three and one half short years ago, when that
Supply
Government returned to power, the prospect of a million or a million and a half unemployed Canadians would have sent shudders down the national spine. They would like Canadians to forget it was normal, just a few short years ago, for high school and college graduates to find work within weeks, not months, after graduating; that it was reasonable for a young couple to expect to own their own home and for the poor to be able to count on a growing economy to produce sufficient revenues to improve their lot. However, I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians are not prone to self-induced amnesia, they cannot and will not easily forget the losses they have suffered and are still suffering, losses of income, of jobs, of homes, of hope, of opportunity.
This Government has failed, Sir. It has failed in its policies and in its commitments to the people of Canada, and the failure of the Government in the first place was in not having avoided the recession which it created. In the second place, its failure was in not having diminished the calamity of a world recession, and its third failure was in not having found a way out of the mess into which it has plunged us all, but especially the poor of this country.
We have before us, Sir, in the Supplementary Estimates, an item of $291 million under the Canada Assistance Plan. That item is in addition to the forecast of just six months ago. It is statutory, not discretionary, because of federal-provincial arrangements. It is needed because the welfare costs incurred by the Provinces at this time are $291 million higher than forecast by the Minister just six months ago. Since inflation has not risen in that period, that means there are about 10 per cent more people on welfare than the Minister forecast. They are on welfare because they have no jobs and their unemployment insurance benefits have terminated.
Let us be under no illusion about this amount, Sir. This is not a magnanimous gesture by a generous and compassionate Government to make life a little easier for the present recipients of social assistance. The money is going to new recipients. But, Sir, there is a cost far greater than this dollar figure would indicate, the human cost. It is the cost represented by the tens of thousands of our fellow Canadians who are just not making it. It is the economic cost to all Canadians of rehabilitation programs, of psychiatric care, of privation, of police services, courts and prisons, costs we will not truly come to know until the lives of the children deprived through the recession unfold before us. The Canadian Mental Health Association and the Family Services Association say that we are foisting costs on the children of the unemployed which we will simply not know for years to come. These children are deprived by and penalized through the policies of this Government.
There is a further cost we may never be able to calculate, that of the thousands of Canadians led into ways of survival beyond the system, outside the pale of what we call civilized society. They are outside the welfare system, outside unemployment insurance benefits, outside of social assistance or

insurance, and into crime and the underground economy. Every Member of this House knows from his or her correspondence and from constituents what it means to be broke, out of work and out of luck in this great country of ours as we approach the winter of 1983. That is what is so tragic, Mr. Speaker. We know the social consequences of hopelessness and poverty. If we have any compassion at all, we can understand the despair and the cries for help which have been triggered.
What concerns me is that when we raise questions with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), the Deputy Prime Minister or the person they put up to answer these questions today, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Lapointe), we seem to get no comprehension at all of the tremendous social costs being created. The Social Planning Council of Toronto has outlined it very clearly in its recent paper "The Poor Get Poorer". They say that poor people generally have less access to adequate nutrition, clothing and housing. They tend to experience more serious health problems and stresses relating to discouraging personal circumstances. The National Council of Welfare directs its attention to the effects of poverty on children. They say inadequate family incomes not only results in material deprivation for children, but increases the likelihod that they would suffer from poor health, malnutrition and family conflicts. Poverty was also linked to poor school attendance, low educational and career aspirations and conflicts with the law.
These people are paying the price, because the people managing the economy, the Government of Canada, have failed consistently and continuously. Most of all, the Government is failing to respond to the indicators which point to a social crisis of enormous magnitude in the future. Currently the income of those on social assistance falls anywhere from 20 per cent to more than 50 per cent below the poverty line. We know that while the poor are getting poorer, they are also getting more numerous. Last year another 550,000 Canadians fell below the poverty line. We know that those hardest hit by the loss of jobs, the reduction of hours, wage cuts and wage freezes, were young families and families headed by women, people who would be the last to benefit from any recovery. The recession has been cruel to all Canadians but crudest of all to those least able to bear its hardships. How can we hope to face the new challenges ahead of us, the challenges of technology, if we cannot meet the problems before us now?
This Government stands condemned, Mr. Speaker, because it cannot deal with the problems of today. It certainly cannot cope with the problems of tomorrow. It cannot deal with the problems of today because of a lack of foresight which brought us into this recession and which created the widespread human suffering and despair seen on every side. The human suffering and despair which the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre simply does not seem to comprehend. The symbol and evidence of that lack of foresight, Mr. Speaker, is with us here today in that increased estimate for the Canada Assistance payments. The Government did not see that once again its policies were going to escalate that payment. How much better if that kind of money could be put into jobs, to create meaningful occupations for these people. It would give them some dignity, allow them to feel they are not living as second-class citizens in their own country and that they are contributing to the betterment of this country.
It is true, Sir, that we will pay that additional sum, because of course we must. Our fellow Canadians need it. But much more than the basic survival which this gives them, they need a Government committed to the economic recovery and prosperity not just of the lucky few in this country, but of all Canadians. It is well past time that they got that kind of Government, and it is not to be found over there on the Government benches today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's message is one that many in this House would not disagree with. We cannot tolerate poverty, we cannot tolerate high unemployment, we have to do things to resolve that situation. Member square the circle of being in favour of enhanced spending on new programs, which she and many in this House are for, with the intent of the motion to condemn the Government for doing precisely that during a period in which we face a world-wide recession of enormous proportions and to which this Government responded by allowing the deficit to rise? How can she stand there and condemn this Government for doing something and still say that she supports the motion which the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) put forward?

Mr. Speaker, what the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council does not seem to understand it that there is a way to bring about increased revenues into the federal coffers, that is to have more people at work; not on unemployment insurance, not on welfare, not on assistance payments, but at work contributing to the country and paying into federal revenues. If the Member would only look at it he would see that the revenues of the federal Government are down this fiscal year by 3 per cent. That is the problem that we have facing us. Naturally, when revenues fall you are going to have greater deficits. We are saying that a Progressive Conservative Government would bring in programs which will create jobs and not ensure, as this Government does, that people remain unemployed and out of the labour force.

Member for Kingston and the Islands agree with the defence critic of her Party who says that we should be moving toward and increase in our defence expenditures from 2 per cent of GNP to 3.5 per cent of GNP at a time when she is saying that we need to put more money where the need is greatest, and that is with the people who have the greatest need in this society? speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
