Exporting our money.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the Hon. Member to elaborate on her answer to the question from my colleague. She said that if she were in government they would have concrete programs to create jobs. What would those programs be?

With regard to job creation 1 would ask the Hon. Member to take a look at where we should be in the next five years. I will give you an example of my own riding, Kingston and The Islands, which has the basis to provide jobs in new technologies. They are not being created there because the training programs for people have not been started by this Government. In this country we are not equipped at all to take advantage of the technological age. That is another example of failure on the part of this Government. We are being surpassed by Japan, France and Singapore in the technological age. That is where jobs would be created. However, before they can be created we need trained human resources.

I think we are getting somewhere. Now we have a concrete expenditure program that the Hon. Member wants. She wants the federal Government to get directly involved in a much higher level of training in terms of the new technologies. Have you put a cost estimate on it? Have you realized that training and education is basically a provincial domain and that your condemnation in this area is aimed directly at your provincial Premier?

Mr. Speaker, now I know why this country, under this Government, will never be able to compete with any other industrialized country as we enter the technological age. If it does not realize that leadership has to come from Government in co-operation with industry, unions and the educational system, he is not talking about the same world that most other countries are living in today. speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Member for Willowdale.

Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing that makes me sick as a politician it is the fact that Members on the other side will stand up and bleed in public to the extent that blood runs over the green rug in this Chamber, and yet will not come up with specific solutions.

What have you done?

November 28, 1983
Supply

Mr. Speaker, we on this side care as much, if not more, about the unemployed, the poor, the senior citizens, the people who suffer the ravages of inflation, and the people who have lost homes, property and income during this recession. The difference is that we are prepared to do something about it. We have seen from the opposite side today motions proposed by the Tories condemning the amount of Government expenditures. That is a condemnation of this Government. Yet we hear the Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) proposing one concrete program involving training in the new technologies, one program that is going to require additional federal expenditures. She did not say that that would immediately reduce the deficit, because she knows it will not. Training is a long-term investment which we make in our young. It is a necessary investment. It is a very valid one. It is one that we are making. I will go on to give you some figures on that. You might disagree and say we are not doing enough. Then I would applaud you for coming forward and saying it is a good program, we should do more of it. That would be an honest approach to dealing with the problem of people out there, rather than trying to make cheap policies on the back of the people who suffered from this recession.
Let us get on to what this resolution really calls for. The resolution states that the lack of the Government's ability to deal with expenditures has caused our financial situation today. According to the Opposition, it is a situation which should be condemned.
I want to establish the basis for the policies that we have adopted and have had in effect for some time and that we see taking us a long time into the future. They are policies which, 1 feel, represent a responsible way to meet the current economic realities.
Our White Paper, which was published on October 14, 1975, said:
The federal government shares the view that the trend of total spending by all governments should not rise more quickly than the trend of the gross national product.
The basis for this policy was then, as it is now, a wise one. It is the philosophy and approach of this Government to adhere to it and to emphasize the primary role that the private sector must play in our country in terms of generating wealth.
Let me go forward eight years from that statement in 1975 to the budget of April, 1983. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said, "This commitment", which we made in 1975, "was met until the recession last year." Since there was a recession, a world-wide recession of which we were a part and in which we suffered severely as Canadians, we broke that policy for a brief period of time. However, our commitment to maintain that trend still remains and we are still within the trend. Let me quote from the budget:
By 1986-87, federal spending will be virtuallly the same size relative to the economy as in 1981-82 before the worst of the recession.
We have taken a very serious approach to dealing with Government expenditures, making sure that Canadians receive
value for the money for which we are the custodian and trustee of the public to spend on their behalf.
I go back to the Glassco Commission on Government Organization in 1962 wherein the primary principle adopted was that we have to let our public servants who are the managers get on with the job of managing. We appointed the Lambert Commission on Financial Management and Accountability. It reported in 1979 and urged that managers be required to manage. It is not only their job but we should be sure that they do it. They should be obliged to pay attention to their respective assigned and acceptable responsibility and to understand that it matters.
We have followed up on what Lambert recommended. I refer Hon. Members and all Canadians to the report issued by the then President of the Treasury Board in 1981 entitled "Accountable Management". Briefly, the conclusion of this report was that the Government has taken the steps necessary to reaffirm control of the public purse. The Government has generated a momentum for continuing reform in financial and human resource management. As well, managers will be required to manage and attention will be paid to results. The Government will be better able to give Canadians value for their money.
We are doing this through a seven point program. First, it involves fiscal plans. We have introduced long-term fiscal plans which are contained in our budgets. They project the results of our initiatives and policies over a five-year period so that Canadians can see where we are going and so that we are not just focusing on the moment but looking for the long-term effects.
Second, we have introduced discipline in the resource allocation process related to the fiscal plan. In other words, we have introduced an envelope program so that various committees of Cabinet are required to have their expenditures kept within an envelope. If we want to introduce new plans within an envelope system in one particular Cabinet committee, the funding must come from the existing programs in that area. In this way we continually renew and get rid of the deadwood. It is a very sound system of financial control within which a Minister, in order to introduce a new program, must go to his fellow Ministers to request funds from their programs in the belief that his program is better for the people of Canada.
The third point concerns a new sense of accountability of the Government to Parliament. We are seeing this through the revised committee system and in the progress of the report on the regulatory reform. We have consultation with the private sector in which it is asked to get involved.
We have a new system of accountability within the Government itself, not only within the envelope program but in internal controls that we have brought into play, including the office of the Comptroller General, which is our creation, and an enhanced role for the Auditor General. Again, it is a Liberal Government that is bringing these tools for fiscal responsibility to bear, to make sure that Canadians are getting value for their tax dollars. We have also introduced accountability and effectiveness in the administration of our financial
November 28, 1983

systems. As well, we have brought in accountability and efficiency in our human resource management and a continuing strategy for reform.
Let me give an example. Opposition Members are continually citing the size of the Public Service. They condemn it and are the ones who are on record as wanting to slash it. They think that the way to achieve efficiency is to chop off large numbers. They would do it by percentages and by eliminating
60,000	public servants.
1 believe we have acted more constructively. In spite of the recession and the need to have programs in place to help those who need the social net during these difficult times, we limited the growth in the public sector, through sound management, to a maximum of about one per cent per year. The size of the Public Service under Treasury Board control today is the same in 1983 as it was in 1976-77. That is not a bad record considering that the expenditures of the federal Public Service have had to increase during that period. I do not know of any other Public Service, provincial or federal throughout the world, that has had this type of record.
Of course, a very important aspect of this debate concerns the size of our total economy that is occupied by governments in Canada. Is government becoming too pervasive? Is it taking over functions which the public sector should not be doing and should be leaving to the private sector? Are we decreasing opportunities for Canadians because of our role as a federal Government? That must be the issue to be addressed by the convoluted resolution of the Opposition today.
Let us look at the size of the involvement of all governments in the Canadian economy. In 1969 in Canada, governments occupied 35 per cent of our gross domestic product. This figure was up to 41 per cent in 1980, which is an increase of 6 per cent. During that period of time our increase was among the smallest of the western industrialized countries. Countries such as Italy, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden have their governments play a much more pervasive role. We are not talking strictly about the federal Government's role but about governments at all levels. With regard to federal Government outlays, as I said earlier, the federal Government has respected that trend line in terms of growth of our expenditures. In 1981-1982 the federal Government's share of the GNP amounted to 20.8 per cent. In 1982-1983, because of the recession, counter cyclical measures to help Canadians during those tough periods, measures which I strongly support, rose to 23.1 per cent.
To 25.8 per cent.
In 1983-1984 they will rise a little bit again to 23.6 per cent.

To 25.8 per cent, according to your own figures.

We will then see a decline, according to our fiscal projections, according to the plans which we responsibly laid before Parliament, to 22.7 per cent.
Try honesty for a change.
Use the national account figures.
Going on to the next year, they will be 22 per cent, and in 1986-1987 that figure will go down to 21.3 per cent.
Use the national account figures.

I am here to say that I am glad we have made the federal intervention at this time to help Canadians who need help most.
In our last budget we devoted S2.4 billion in new expenditures to the Special Recovery Capital Project to help Canadians bring on the infrastructure, accelerate implementation of capital projects that will benefit all of us over the long term but would not have been brought on because of the recession or would not have been brought on as quickly. These were brought on to create that type of economic wealth building system which we need in Canada. The amount of $2.4 billion was allocated to create employment immediately. What I think is even more important, and what I am even more proud of, is that we have brought on another $2.4 billion in tax expenditures, tax incentives to the private sector, tax incentives to business to go about doing the job which it does best and which it can do better than any other body in Canada, namely that of creating jobs. That $2.4 billion in tax incentives is being expended in a variety of ways.
1 want to go through some of them because I want Canadians to know where their tax dollars are going. I am proud of where they are going. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was talking about having to bring Canadians up to scratch in terms of the new technologies. We projected R and D expenditures of 1.5 per cent of GNP in 1979, and we will meet that commitment probably one year ahead of schedule. Many of us might have the feeling that we should have set a higher target. I would not disagree with those who argue for a higher target, but what have we done in terms of R and D expenditures?
In 1980 our tax incentives for research and development, scientific research, amounted to about $181 million. These benefits were enjoyed by about 343 firms in Canada. They cost us in lost taxes about $120 million. In our 1983 budget we took R and D tax incentives to the private sector, ones which were the most generous of any industrialized nation in the world, and we enhanced them even further in such a way that small business can use them and attract new capital investment. We made a tax shelter available so investors in new enterprises involved in high-tech can attract the equity capital necessary. Those firms that want to go out and increase their expenditures and increase their physical plant and equipment can do it now and get accelerated write-offs.

What have we done in scientific activities alone? We increased our expenditures last year as a federal Government from $2.9 billion to $3.2 billion, a ten per cent increase. That is a very constructive way of meeting some Of the problems which the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands was talking about. But did she give us credit for that? No, she just stood up and bled all over the floor without coming up with anything concrete or constructive.
I think I have heard you say that already. That was on page 1 of your speech, Jim; you forgot to turn the page.
Let us look at the deficit. We have a problem, and we all agree with it. All of us wish we did not need to have a deficit.
We don't have to either. You are spending more than you take in.
What caused that deficit? It was caused essentially by a decline in tax revenues during the recession. For the 15 year period prior to 1981-
Prior to 1975.

-business profits contributed about 11.2 per cent of our Gross National Product. In 1981 that figure declined to 10 per cent. In 1982, the worst year of the recession, we reached a post-war low of 6.2 per cent. In other words, during the recession businesses did not have the profits and, therefore, did not have the income to pay their taxes. This recession was marked by very high inflation, high interest, falling demand and dwindling profits. What have we done about it? I have talked about the $2.4 billion in Special Capital Recovery Projects. I have talked about the $2.4 billion to the private sector through tax incentives to get it going. We have also done some other things. We have the Indexed Securities Investment Plan. We have tax treatment of business losses for business. We have increased the loss carry forward from three years back to seven years forward. We now have an 11-year period over which losses can be absorbed instead of a seven-year period. We have cut back on some of the energy taxes, including the lORT and the PGRT taxes. We made mining depletion allowances available. You could write them off against other income. That is an incentive to increase investment in that sector.
Let me come to small business. Here we have the special recovery refundable investment tax crecit, a 40 per cent credit for small business.
Farmers get a 14-year period during which their losses can be absorbed-three years back and ten years forward. The Farm Credit Corporation has its resources expanded to $150 million. This was a $100 million increase in its time of difficulty and it means that farmers will be able to bet loans at 4 per cent below the going rate.
What did we do in the housing area? I am very proud of the initiatives of this Government. They were worked out in consultation with the Toronto Home Builders Assciation,
HUDAC Ontario and the Canadian housing industry. This is the way programs should be worked out. They were worked out to meet the needs of that industry. It was demonstrated to us that for every new house going up, a very desirable social objective, we create 2.1 person years of work. How was this done? We did it through a series of $3,000 grants. For each $3,000 grant, not only did we get 2.1 person years of direct employment and a home but we generated $10,600 of new tax revenue in the first year of construction of that house. That is a creative use of public money in order to create jobs and achieve the socially desirable results. I am very proud of the housing programs we have undertaken. I thing that in the future if we want to be constructive we will look to creating even more social housing for Canadians. This is a very pressing need. I am very proud of the programs we have introduced that give Canadians who cannot otherwise afford good housing the types of things we have demonstrated we are capable of doing in the past and that we are going to devote even more resources to in the future.

I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but his allotted time lapsed some time ago. I had assumed he was concluding his remarks and that is why I let him continue. Are there any questions, comments, answers?

We must congratulate the Hon. Member as Chairman of the House Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, Mr. Speaker. Would he agree with the Prime Minister's statement in his press conference on August 13, 1969 when he said:
We'd soon be on the road to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control.

Mr. Speaker, of course I agree with that. This is the whole gist of why this debate has been so unfounded. We have been doing things since that comment in 1969 to bring Government spending under control. We have a whole new system of fiscal management; the five-year plans we have been projecting, the six-year plans in our budgets. We have brought into effect the office of the Comptroller-General. The Auditor General has an enhanced role to play. Parliamentary committees, through the revised estimates, have better access to every type of expenditure being made so there is accountability of the Government to Parliament. We have the enveloped system, which is one of the most effective ways of ensuring that we do not bring in new programs just to be filed on top of old ones. We have a way of eliminating poor programs and replacing them with better ones.
The size of the federal Government's role in our economy, as demonstrated by the figures, has held pretty well firm throughout the period 1969 to now, hovering around 21 per cent of our GNP. Barring a recession, we had hoped to have it down to about 19 per cent by now. Because of that recession, we have undertaken to create social nets to protect people. Without them, it would have been a travesty in human terms and many people would have suffered. If you came to me and said, "Peterson, the Liberal Government has not created
November 28, 1983

enough social nets, it should be spending more to protect people during this difficult period", you might have received a little sympathy from this side with that type of resolution.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Wil-lowdale is totally misleading when he says that the Government is not building on old programs. One of the tragedies we face today is that there is no zero base budgeting going on. The A base in the estimates is the old program. If you go to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), he will tell you there is no zero base budgeting going on in old programs. That is why we are out of control. This House and our committee system is not doing the work it should be doing, examining and forcing zero-based budgeting. The only zero base budgeting is in the Department of National Defence. The rest of it is incremental additions of indexing CPI on top of old programs. That is what the debate is all about. When the Hon. Member for Willowdale tries to imply that we are going back and examining old programs, he is totally wrong. That is not true to fact.

Mr. Speaker, I hate to inform the Hon. Member for Capilano that under the envelope system, if we are going to add a new program, we have to get it out of the same envelope. If you have an envelope with X number of programs and you want to add X plus one, you have to take it out of an existing program. That is the discipline that is imposed.
You have not done that.

The Hon. Member says we are not doing that. If Members opposite want to see a big cut in the federal role being played, I challenge them to come forward to us with concrete programs that we can cut out. I have heard nothing about programs that they want to add. I suggest they come to us with programs they want to cut out. If they feel they are wasteful, they may find a very receptive audience on this side, but stop coming forward to us with increased expenditures such as the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands did, saying we have not spent enough to help those who have suffered.
Let me respond to what we have done in this period in terms of job creation. I will never tell any person that it is acceptable that we have an unemployment level that exceeds 11 per cent in Canada. This is our greatest challenge. Instead of just bleeding about it, we have been doing something.
You created it.

The Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands says we created that position. The fact is that we have created the best record of job creation in this country of any western industrialized nation since 1970. In the last 12 months alone we have created 350,000 new jobs. Since 1970 we have created 50 per cent more jobs in Canada than we had 13 years ago, this during a period when West Germany has suffered a 2 per cent decline in the number of jobs.

If you are comparing us to our neighbours, bring in those facts and recognize the fact that all the private analysts are now saying that Canada is better poised to come out of this recession better than any other western country, that our record has been very good. Those are the facts. Interest rates are down. Our six and five program has done something about inflation. We are creating jobs, even though they are not being created fast enough. Tell us how to create more jobs more quickly without increasing the deficit. Tell us how to do it by increasing the deficit reasonably so that we get value for our dollar. That is the type of constructive debate Canadians deserve in this House rather than the petty politics I have heard here today.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have to correct another very misleading statement made by the Hon. Member for Willowdale.

When he had the portfolio of Industry, Trade and Commerce, he authorized a study of the steel bar mill in the Windsor area, which 1 understand cost about $750,000. That is an example of waste. At the time he requested the study, Stelco and Co-Steel the other major producers of steel bar in Canada were operating at 40 per cent capacity; today they are operating at between 40 and 60 per cent capacity, but that will slide back to 40 per cent during the winter months. How can the present Minister say that the government is still studying that problem when he knows that the industry is in a surplus position at the moment?
Let us deal now with the aerospace industry which the Government thinks is a winner, although it has been incredibly bad at picking winners and losers. Last year it blew $2 billion on Canadair and de Havilland. It produced a toy jet for corporate executives at Canadair and a small airliner at de Havilland. The two airlines that were the largest purchasers of the Dash 7 aircraft have gone into bankruptcy. That speaks well for a small number of passenger airplanes.
We have seen the Government pick the wrong things, and now it has decided to pick on helicopters. Why does it think it can be successful in this after the losses it has shown? Not only

did it pick helicopters but it put the original one up at Mirabel in an effort to justify, for the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc), that the expropriation in that area was a good idea in the first place. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext: Don't rewrite history.

The Government is always trying to justify its past expenditures, but it has not made any sound expenditures as yet. It put the Bell helicopter at Mirabel, surrounded by farmers. There is no technical expertise in that area and the people do not want any industry there. They just want to run their farms in an area which contains 1 per cent of Quebec's class one arable land. The Government wants to put the helicopters there so that it can justify the $1 billion that was spent to build a surplus airport. These must be dandy helicopters if they need that much runway.
I support the point made by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) in relation to the $500 million that is going to Pratt & Whitney. It is amazing how well that company has done in East Hartford, Connecticut, United States. I happen to have gone to school there. That company was very successful post-war and it still is. It is amazing how much it has done without Government subsidies. I admit it has had National Defence contracts to develop new technology. That is why the Americans are so much further ahead than we are. Our Government does not even contemplate that.
The Japanese leave it to the private sector to decide who should win and who should lose. I wish the Minister of State for Economic Development would read papers such as the Japan Robot News and that published by the Yano Research Institute. They would give him some lead information about where to go. I do not believe he knows how to get out of this dilemma.
We have to create jobs and we have to create wealth. The redistribution of wealth has not worked because there is none left to redistribute. We have to create wealth for jobs and new industries, and we have to stop these give-away programs wherever the Government sees fit.
Since 1968, manufacturing productivity in Canada has increased at the second slowest pace of any industrialized
nation. There are no incentives. Since 1979, $16.5 billion of investment capital has left the country because the Government is hostile to the private sector which has not been provided with incentives. From 1977 to 1982 productivity stood still and since 1982 it has been reduced by 2.8 per cent, the worst rate of any country in the world.
I should like to remind Hon. Members opposite of what some Members of the Government have said. In 1980-81, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), in his former capacity, said that in order to achieve the essential reduction in the deficit great restraint over expenditures had been required. Hon. Members opposite speak words but they do not mean anything. In 1981-82, the same Minister said that "we must reduce our deficit and our borrowing requirements substantially". You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that it was the National Energy Program that brought this country to a standstill. In 1982-83, the same Minister said that interest rates would rise even more and that Canada would price itself out of world markets.
Our export sales of manufactured goods have decreased so dramatically that we are no longer competitive, Mr. Speaker. We are not highly productive and we have lost our sense of innovation and of private enterprise.
In April, 1983, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said that he was presenting a fiscally responsible budget. Mr. Speaker, no budget that has increased our expenditures by up to $100 billion where the deficit is $31 billion, is a responsible budget. In 1968-69 our national debt was $18 billion; today it is $150 billion, and next year it will be ten times that or 1,000 per cent of what it was.
In 1968 Canada had 5.744 per cent of world trade, but in 1981 it had 3.8 per cent. In 1968 we exported more than Japan did; today we export half of what Japan exports. That is because Japan put plans and policies in place. It did it with thought. It did it with policy. Particularly, Mr. Speaker, it gave initiatives to the private sector which this Government has failed to do and, as a result, we do not have the jobs. We have this tremendous deficit because we do not have the industry. We have two million people unemployed who are drawing on society. Their costs, according to the Canadian Mental Health Association, could amount to $50 billion.
I believe this debate today is very important in order to make the people aware that this Government is misguided and misdirected. Its priorities are not where they should be. It is our responsibility, as the Opposition, before we form the next government, to let the people know what damage this Government has done to Canadians and the debt it has built up for every man, woman and child in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions, comments. Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this debate. The Conservative motion is that the House agree without reservation with a statement made by
November 28, 1983

the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1969 about the country being on the road to financial disaster if nothing is done to bring spending under control. The motion goes on to call on the Government to initiate policies to avoid that prediction. In other words, it calls for tight fiscal restraint. I have a question 1 would like to put to Hon. Members of the House, especially to my Conservative colleagues on my right. I see the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) looking up. I will put the question to her. Who said, "In spite of the very substantial deficit with which we are confronted, programs in very important areas necessary for the development of the country are being cut"? That speaker gave five examples, medicare, post-secondary education, scientific research, funding for the arts and international aid. Who was it who stood in this House and said that? I will give you a further hint, Mr. Speaker. The speech was made within a year of that quote from the Prime Minister. I will ask the last Hon. Member who spoke. Who said that?
I bet I did not say it.

I will tell you who said it. It was the Hon. Robert L. Stanfield who was the Leader of the Conservative Party and Leader of the Opposition. Is it not incredible that the Conservative Party offers a motion today which relates back to 1969? That was the era when "Wacky Bennett" had just won an election in British Columbia, Jean Lesage had just resigned in Quebec. There was a federal-provincial finance conference in Quebec which was supposed to be a watershed that year. The motion goes back to 1969 and quotes the Prime Minister, who was supposed to be against further federal spending, suggesting the Prime Minister should live by that today, when around the same period Robert L. Stanfield stood up in the Commons and said, "You really cannot cut federal spending because if you do, you are going to cut back medicare, post-secondary education, scientific research, funding to the arts and international aid." Is that not incredible? Why does the Conservative Party not get its act together?
The previous speaker said that the Government is misguided and misdirected. I cannot think of a Party which is more misguided and more misdirected than the Conservative Party when it has speaking for it, supposedly, a Red Tory, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, who would agree, I believe, with what Robert Stanfield said, and the ultra-blue Tory, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), and the ultra rightwing Tory, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). That Party cannot have it both ways if it is going to govern Canada. Which is it going to be?
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the spending of this Government is not under control. The question surely is, where is that spending going? The motion is simply designed to embarrass the Liberal Government-and that is pretty easy to do-and it has backfired and embarrassed the Tories. If one looks at Robert Stanfield's speech, one will see that it really makes the Official Opposition look silly in introducing this kind of text today, when there was so much more it could have put in a motion. I suggest that that Party look at the previous motion which the
Supply
Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands brought forward. She talked about unemployment and the new kind of economy we have to face in Canada.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are incompetent in managing the economy, but that does not have to be said in the House of Commons. One can ask a cab driver down the street, he will say the same thing. The method of the Liberal Government is really, "If it moves, throw money at it. If if has votes, throw more money at it. If it is one of your friends in an industry which is in trouble, give it more money". We give $2 billion in petroleum grants in this country. For what? For companies to have 105 per cent write-offs. We give money for unemployment insurance in this country, and the reason we do that is because of Government policy. That is how it tackled inflation, by slowing down the economy completely and by creating unemployment.
We are really dealing with a Government which has run out of ideas. Modern North American Liberalism is finished. It does not stand for anything. It zigs and it zags and it tries to build on the old programs. The Throne Speech which is coming up will tag a few things on to the Unemployment Insurance Program, move a little bit here, have a commission on medicare. But it is failing. And I say this to the Liberals who are listening: watch what the Conservatives are saying in North America. I disagree with them, but they are getting some support because of those Hon. Members have been saying what they believe in strongly, and they are not zigging and zagging. It falls to us on the left, as a Social Democratic Party, also to say what we believe in strongly. If that happens, you will find that there will be two major political Parties in Canada come the next election, the Conservatives and the New Democrats.

Absolutely! It is the same in Quebec.

Yes . . . wait and see!

I would just like to say one more thing to the Conservatives and let them consider whether they are for Mr. Stanfield or for the Hon. Member for Capilano. Perhaps as a little forerunner of what we may see from a Conservative government, I will quote from a book called, "The Contenders-A Tory quest for power". On page 86 of the book, I notice the new Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) says, in terms of what his government is going to be like, the spending of his government and the political appointments of his government, and I quote:
I am going to dance with the ones who hrung me.
I hat means l ories that's what this is all about.
Va dance with the lady what brung ya.

That means, of course, that he is going to continue the same patronage-infested system in Canada. The harbours will be built in a different riding in the Maritimes. It is the same kind of old system which we have to get away from. There may be a few changes, less money on social service, more money for armaments.
Tell us about Manitoba!

1 can see the new Leader of the Opposition now, who really is just a poodle for Conrad Black and the boys in Toronto. Is that not who is really calling the shots? When Conrad wants to take Brian for a walk and tell him what the new policy will be of the government, that is what the policy will be. He is simply the poodle. It is too bad, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Robert Stanfield is not back in this House, because there is a man who understood what a deficit meant. There was a man who understood that you did not focus on a deficit. You focused on the programs. What does it matter, really, what the public debt is, although we should be concerned about that. If people are working and if the economy is prosperous, will people lose sleep over whether the deficit is $10 billion or $11 billion? No, Mr. Speaker.
We are faced with a high technological society, with rapid technological change. The previous speaker might want to listen for a minute. If he hopes to get into Government he will have to deal with the fact that we have a society which is rapidly replacing people with machines, not just blue collar workers but white collar workers, middle management, secretaries and so on, especially women. We are going to get more of this.
The Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) said "we have created jobs". But what kind of jobs? "We have spent money", he said, but what have we spent that money on? The jobs being created are low-paying service jobs. We are losing the middle rung jobs. In five years we are going to have a society in which a few people at the top make big money and the great mass of the people are down at the bottom. We are going to lose the middle class. It is not just a question of bleeding for the unemployed or special groups who have problems. We are in real danger of losing our middle class, and I would think Members of Parliament would be very interested in that.
What can be done, Mr. Speaker? 1 do not think we should focus on cutting the deficit. We should focus on an industrial policy for Canada. We need economic democracy. It seems to me the Conservatives and Liberals have adopted the philosophy of "leave it to the magic of the marketplace". As 1 say that, I am looking over at the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston). Let me suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that will not happen. First of all, Canada is a mixed economy. When you have problems at the public level, the civil service or Crown corporations, you do not throw them out like the baby with the bath water, you reform them. You do not stand up and attack Government per se. We saw in British
Columbia that people were very politicized as the general strike approached. Like the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble), people attack the whole notion of the Public Service. They say it is not a job if you are a public servant. It is not a job if you are a garbage man, police officer, fireman, a clerk sending out cheques or a nurse looking after old people. Somehow that is not a job. Well, it is and we should talk about that. You cannot say these are not jobs.
Getting back to my theme, Mr. Speaker, you have to have an industrial policy. We have to get labour, government and industry together. Not at that conference that the Minister had, the Canada Tomorrow Conference, although it was well intentioned. But if you want to get labour into it, you have to assure the working people of this country that they are going to be protected in some way from change. They are not stupid, they know they are going to suffer from change and there will be job lay-offs. But they have to be protected. The Government should look at some of the work of Robert Reich, a Harvard economist. He said:
Unless members of a democratic society are persuaded the benefits and burdens of change are being allocated more or less evenly, they will resist change, and their resistence will prove extremely powerful.
I saw that in British Columbia where the Government tried to come in with draconian restraint measures and the people resisted. They were pushed to a point at which they resisted. Why should the worker not have a say in technological change or safety in the work place? Why should the worker not have some say? Why should he not be put into a training program which will take him to a new level? Why should the safety net not be expanded? That is what the Canadian middle class is worried about. They are prepared to accept change, they know it is coming. They do not want to sit here and debate deficits or debate 1969 quotes, especially one which goes one way and to which Robert Stanfield takes exactly the opposite viewpoint. That is silly. They want us to make it easier for them to leave their homes and go where the jobs are. They want us to look for policies where the human virtues of participation, equality and security can be brought forward. That is the direction of the future economy of Canada. But let us not go back to look at what Trudeau said in August, 1969. Let us look ahead. Let us look to policies which will deal with this high-tech revolution which is coming fast. Let us make sure that it is not just Conrad Black and the boys who benefit from change. Let us make sure there is a recovery for everyone.
I suggest the Government look at some of the ideas I put forward today. 1 hope that in their next motion the Conservatives will give these people something to shoot at rather than these silly motions which really do not have very much substance to them.

the same as yours, that the vote was to have been called at 5.45. I have no trouble accommodating the hon. gentleman for Provencher (Mr. Epp). I will speak for ten minutes and then relinquish the floor to whoever may want it on the opposite side of the House.
The Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) mentioned in his address that the esteem of this House in the eyes of the public has fallen to an all-time low. Most Canadians find that this House is irrelevant, not only to the life of Canadians in general, but to their lives specifically. I would point out to the hon. gentleman that the reason for that does not lie with the spiralling deficit, which he attacked so vigorously this afternoon, but can be found in the type of motion which has absorbed the valuable time of this House all day. The deficit is an archaic political issue. It was raised about four or five years ago. It tended to shape political behaviour or attitudes in the 1979 election. Since 1980 not very many people are paying attention to it. The reason they are not paying attention to it, quite frankly, is that they know that in a recessionary period you cannot eliminate the deficit or roll it back to any significant degree.
The Opposition, nonetheless, has decided in its wisdom to resurrect this issue and parade it once again before the House and, hopefully, before the media and the Canadian public, in an effort to try to recapture some of the lost political ground that will be revealed in the next Gallup poll.
We are hoping.

If this argument worked once, four or five years ago, then, by golly, it just might work again. If we can revive it, if we can renovate it, if we can still address it as forcefully today as we did originally, then maybe we can hold on to those voters that we feel slipping from our grasp because we really do not have any specific, concrete policies in this Party or in this leadership. Mr. Speaker, I think the ploy is that transparent. They are desperately looking for the old winning issues that brought them victory in the old glory days of 1977, 1978 and 1979, when it felt good to bash Grits and finally win an election. It just might win again. Why, we even have more facts and figures this time. We have different and better speakers. Who knows, we may be able to ride this again into another electoral victory.
I wish the Opposition could see themselves as others see them when they try to make political points with this archaic, rusty old rhetorical issue. For heaven's sake, they cannot even agree on the nature of the debate in this House. One person gets up and says, "Cut." The other person gets up and says, "Well, perhaps cut but, by golly, we should be thinking of spending too." So you have got cutters and spenders in the same Party.
Shame.

Not only are they inconsistent in where they are coming from and where they want to go, Mr. Speaker, but they do not even know their facts in this issue. The Hon. Member gets up and asks why this Government does not act

more like the Governments of Japan, France, Singapore and Governments like that. Why do they not? When you point out to her that those are high deficit Governments, she did not know that. Someone else gets up and asks if we realize that Government spending has gone from 33.7 per cent to 47.3 per cent of disposable income. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, he fails to inform the House, and presumably the Canadian public, that that increase in expenditures did not result exclusively, or even primarily, from the expenditures of the Government of Canada. They ask the Canadian public, through the media that reports the deliberations of this House, what they have as a result of those expenditures. What have you received? Nothing. All is decay around you. We live in a wasteland. You have got nothing. You have been robbed. Mr. Speaker, they say it with such passion, with such conviction, with such vigour in their voices that most Canadians say, "By God, they must be right. No one could speak like that. No one could speak with that authority if that were not the case. By golly, we must not have got very much from them. They are right."
I invite you and others, Mr. Speaker, to look at the society around us to see what is out there. You do not have to be a brilliant academician to test the validity of that argument. Just open the door and walk around your neighbourhood and see what it is like and how it has changed in the last 10 or 15 years while the Liberals were in power. What do you find? You find beautiful senior citizens' residences everywhere paid for by, in large measure, the Government of Canada. You find one of the best educational systems anywhere in the world funded primarily, at the post secondary school level, by the Government of Canada. Walk further and you will find the finest hospital system in the world funded again, through provincial authorities, by the Government of Canada. Everywhere you look, Mr. Speaker, no matter what part of Canada or what community you live in, you will find tangible, concrete evidence of what that deficit has given Canadians. It has given Canadians the finest social system in the western world. That is something that all of us in this House can be proud of.
After they talk about the wastefulness, Mr. Speaker, they then say, "We have solutions. We are not negative carpers or shrill harbingers of doom and gloom. We have solutions." The first solution proposed this afternoon was to have this House adopt the report of the Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. States. But the deficit down there is far larger than it is here. I would argue that committees of that sort, however well intentioned, are quite frankly not the issue.
Another solution is to elect a Tory government. The Tories say to elect them because they know the value of a dollar. But every Conservative leadership candidate went into debt during his or her leadership campaign.
I beg your pardon? That is a Liberal lie.

I take that back, Mr. Speaker. I stand corrected. Everyone of them but one. But all the major candidates, the serious ones, were in debt. They went hopelessly and shamefully into debt.

If Canadians entrust the Government of this fair land in the hands of the Party that now forms the Official Opposition, Mr. Speaker, they will be making the gravest and most irresponsible mistake they could ever make, if they think that electing them would solve the economic problems of the country.

The quotation which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave us on August 13, 1969, was: "We would soon be on the road to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control." That is one of the few accurate statements the Prime Minister has made in the last 14 years.
I have just two other statements which he also made. This statement was made in January of 1980 when he made a solemn commitment. I quote from the Prime Minister in Toronto-the fountain of financial rectitude is Toronto, of course-when he promised to, "manage more rigorously the nation's finances in order to make more effective use of the taxpayers' money."
A final quotation of the Prime Minister is from the Toronto Star, the Liberal Bible, on February 10, 1980. The Prime Minister said, "I want to manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would in fact come down because the economy would be administered in a sounder way ." Well,
November 28, 1983

interest rates after that went from 11 per cent to 23 per cent before they started to come down again.
Those are three of the economic statements of the world's elder statesman who is now going about the world making statements in another field. If his statements on this other interest of his, the peace interest, are as accurate and as full of fruition as his statements have been with respect to the Government's finances in Canada, the Canadian economy and interest rates in Canada, all I can tell you is, God help the world.
The worst advice 1 could give the Hon. Member who just concluded is to be himself or to continue to be himself. This country has been operating in the red for so long under the Government that the public accounts resemble a slaughter house. Not only is its deficit this year $31.3 billion, three times what it was in 1979-80, when we were in office and having to deal with the results of Liberal deficits for that year and the previous year, the Auditor General finds that there is a $5.3 billion hidden deficit. 1 am not making it up. I point this out to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader, although I am not sure whether he reads or not. Is the Government spending money wisely? I hold up another clipping of just several days ago entitled "Kaplan accused of spending $43,000 to spruce up image." The unthinkable sprucing the unspruceable. There is $43,000 being spent by a Cabinet Minister to spruce up his image. We multiply that by the total number of Cabinet Ministers, because they are all sprucing up their images as well. They are trying to spruce up the unspruceable. They are trying to goose the ungooseable, not only spruce the unspruceable. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) is shocked by the ungooseable or the unspruceable. 1 do not blame her.
I want to refer now to the Government's greatest growth. The greatest growth it has had in the 18 or 19 years it has been in power is shown in the fiscal plan that was presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on April 19. I refer you to page 3 where it states:
Debt grew 26.6 per cent in 1982-83 and it is projected to grow a further 26 per cent this year.

The financial requirements, which is the borrowing the Government makes to meet these deficits, will be approximately 6.9 per cent of the GNP this year. That is the record of the Government. Everything else declined except the public debt. The total amount of goods and services produced by the country's economy declined over the last two or three years. The total number of people working declined savagely over the last two or three years. But the debt continues to grow. For what purpose? It has not achieved either growth in the economy or growth in employment.
This is a 7D government. There are seven Ds comprised of equal parts; debt, deception, duplicity, deviousness, desperation, despotism and finally decrepitude. When one looks across the Chamber at the end of an Opposition day, one sees, in all its splendour, decrepitude unfolding before one. The Government is decrepit. Its policies are decrepit. Its debt is decrepit.
It is now engaging only in duplicity and deviousness in the desperate attempt to prevent someone else from forming a government to try to make this country one of growth, promise and hope. Again, it does not have the decency or good will even now to get out of office and call an election. It is clinging by its fingernails, toenails and its hangnails, afraid to go to the Governor General and ask him to dissolve the House, while half the crowd is out travelling around the world in the hope they will be forgotten before they return home so that people will forget what they have and have not done.
1 just have enough time to remind the House of one area of growth, which is loans and loan guarantees. We now have 19.1 billion in loans to the private sector by this Government and provincial Governments, 74 per cent of which is federal. There is $29.4 million in guarantees and loans to private bodies around this country by all 11 Governments, 97 per cent of which is federal. They include such fantastic companies as the Maislin Corporation-amazing Maislin. The friends of the Minister of Finance are among the latest to receive guarantees. One can only marvel that the Canadian public is not in here today ignoring the rules of this House and applauding us, making the Chamber rock with applause, as we attempt to point out how this Government has broken its promises in public spending, in public debt incurment, in every area we care to look at. The disastrous, decrepitudinous collection of twits that only an election can give the Canadian public-have I unanimous consent to continue, Mr. Speaker?
Oh, oh!
-that only a dissolution of the House can give us the chance to rectify this wrong.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-PROVISIONS DEALING WITH HATE LITERATURE
CRIMINAL CODE-PROVISIONS DEALING WITH HATE LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of participating in this debate tonight as a result of the question I posed to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Mac-Guigan) on November 22, 1983 as recorded on page 29079 of Hansard. The question arose from The Globe and Mail news story that morning which suggested that Criminal Code omnibus amendments due early this year or early next year would include changes to deal more effectively with hate propaganda in our Criminal Code.
In asking the question of the Minister of Justice whether those reports were true, I also wanted to know whether the need for an Attorney General to give permission for the laying of a charge of hate mongering would also be withdrawn from the Criminal Code. I must say I was rather disappointed in the vagueness of the response from the Minister. I do appreciate the constraints he faces as a member of cabinet, that he cannot at random announce decisions that have been taken, although regretfully the suggestion was there in the newspaper and yet here in Parliament we were not graced with a response. However, I do hope that as he indicated the Government is moving in this direction.
This issue, the way our law can deal with hate in our country, is of great importance to our society, particularly following the establishment of our own Charter of Rights. The sooner these amendments we hear spoken of in the press, that may well be under consideration by cabinet, are acted upon the better.
I should say, and 1 believe most Members of this House would agree with me, that this is a country of immense tolerance, and yes, there are other countries that have records of tolerance for intolerance far worse than our own but I believe we have no reason at all to be complacent about the current situation in Canada. Certainly our history points out discrimination by the state itself-Government and Parliament-as well as by Canadians. For example, the Chinese people who originally immigrated to this country to assist in the building of the railway were not allowed to have women accompany them, including wives; there was the need for a fee in order to have a man's wife join him in this country, and there is the fact that women of Chinese origin were not allowed to vote in Canada until well after the second World War. We had black slaves in this country in the nineteenth century. Japanese-Canadians, faithful, good citizens who happened to be of Japanese origin, lost all their worldly possessions except what could be carried in a suitcase at a time of crisis during World War II, and were removed to camps. That is just one more example.
Even more important in contemporary terms, there are indications in Canada of a serious problem involving the hate of some Canadians for other Canadians based simply on race. Canada today is a major source of hate literature, distributed around the world as well as here in Canada. That material has been brought to the attention of various Members of Parliament by the Canadian Jewish Congress. In our newspapers, almost daily, there are examples of incidents of racism against Canadians, largely those who are visibly obvious to the larger society which is white. This country can only work if governments take the lead in breaking down barriers in education, in helping people understand each other better in order to get along as Canadians, and also in changing laws that now aid and abet intolerance to the point of creating real anguish for many good Canadians.
As a former journalist, Mr. Speaker, I agree that freedom of speech is fundamental to a healthy democracy but, no more than society would allow the preaching of insurrection of our state itself should it allow the preaching of insurrection to the principles of tolerance in our society and in our new Constitution. Hate that tears at the ability of honest, good Canadians to live in peace and without fear is every bit as damaging and wrong as attacks on our democracy itself.
If free speech is the freedom to tear away the principles of our Charter, then in the name of one freedom we will destroy the others in that Charter. Individuals must remain free to express their views, no matter how unpalatable those views may be to another, so long as that freedom of expression does not in itself lead to pain and real suffering for other Canadians
November 28, 1983

who are innocent of any wrongdoing. That is the essence of my concern. I hope the Government will not be long in responding to a situation that scars the very essence of our new Charter of Rights.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul-Andre Masse (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-PROVISIONS DEALING WITH HATE LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) to reply to the question raised by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Fleming) regarding Criminal Code provisions dealing with hate literature. 1 think his questions are quite appropriate and timely.
Canada is a multicultural society. This is an undeniable fact which is now formally recognized in our Constitution and one which is welcomed by a vast majority of Canadians. Nevertheless, this reality is one which some individuals and groups find distressful. This attitude may result in overt or covert discrimination, and even acts of vandalism or violence. Many federal and provincial agencies are working to demonstrate the important values which flow from the multicultural nature of our country. They seek to bring about a progressive change in the views of those individuals who are prejudiced against visible minorities and other groups in society. This objective is yet to be attained. Therefore, the law continues to play an important role in the protection of various disadvantaged groups against discrimination.
There are several statutes which provide protection and relief to the members of visible minorities who have been discriminated against. This evening, however, I would like to discuss the provisions of the Criminal Code which deal with hate propaganda. These provisions are found in Part VI, Offences against the Person and Reputation, of the Code. More specifically, 281.1 and 281.2(1) and (2) deal with hate propaganda. The first section makes it an offense to promote or advocate genocide. The second makes it an offence to publicly incite hatred against an identifiable group, and the last section is directed at those who promote hatred by communicating statements in public.
Recently, minority groups have expressed their concerns about the lack of prosecutions under the hate propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code. They point to a growth in the prevalence of hate literature and suggest that the protection offered by the Code be improved in several ways.
Some of these suggestions include removing the element of wilfulness in the offence of promotion of hartred; doing away with certain statutory defences currently available to individuals charged with a hate propaganda offence; allowing prosecutions for promotion of hatred without the prior consent of the provincial Attorney General; and, as has also been suggested by some, that historical misrepresentation or the denial of historical events be made an offence if used to promote hatred. With the exception of the last suggestion, the Minister is currently giving careful consideration to all of these recommendations.
Adjournment Debate
! am inclined to believe that the maintenance of harmonious relationships between the various racial, ethnic and religious components of our society warrants a strengthening of the protection against incitement to hatred found in the Code.
With respect to the last recommendation, the issue of historical denial, we are somewhat hesitant to expressly incorporate this notion into the hate propaganda provisions of the Code. The implications of such a proposal are far-reaching. First, historical facts frequently depend upon the perspective from which one views the past. There are numerous incidents in history which are disputed by individuals and groups. Many of these incidents are not clearly defined or cannot be proven. That is why we believe that the courts are not the appropriate forum in which to resolve questions of this nature. Second, we believe that a prosecution under the existing provision could now be attempted against anyone who promoted hatred against an identifiable group on the basis of historical denial. Last, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression.
As you already know, Mr. Speaker, Cabinet approved the creation of a special parliamentary committee to deal with this matter, and I believe that we should wait until that committee presents its report before making further recommendations.

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-CRITERIA GOVERNING CONTRACTS- UNEMPLOYMENT AT PORT WELLER. (B) SUBSIDY TO MARINE INDUSTRIES IN SOREL, P.Q.
SHIPBUILDING-CRITERIA GOVERNING CONTRACTS- UNEMPLOYMENT AT PORT WELLER. (B) SUBSIDY TO MARINE INDUSTRIES IN SOREL, P.Q.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 31 last, I raised two questions with respect to the awarding of the six Class 1,100 icebreaker contracts. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Lapointe) responded by saying that the lowest bid is the criterion which is always used by the Government in a public call for tenders. However, the Minister was contradicted by a statement which came from his own office that very day.
That release clearly stated that national socio-economic considerations had to be a factor in virtually any contract the Government awarded. Of course, socio-economic considerations have to be factors in order to be consistent with the budget speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in April of this year. He said that earth will be moved, steel will be rigged and concrete will be poured in all parts of the country. The $630 million spent to upgrade and modernize the Canadian Coastguard fleet was to relieve regional disparity. However, nothing was said about the Government's selectivity program.
Adding insult to injury, the Minister's statement concluded by citing the reduction of unemployment as a key objective in the awarding of federal contracts. If unemployment is a factor at all, then St. Catharines-Niagara should be a prime candidate for favourable consideration.
For the past two months, St. Catharines-Niagara has led the country in urban unemployment rates. Last month, 26,000 people were out of work in the Niagara area and that figure is expected to rise over the next few months. Port Weller dry-

November 28, 1983
Adjournment Debate
docks, once the most efficient and competitive yard in the country and once an employer of some 950 ship workers, now employs less than 200. That Port Weller drydocks was not included in the new ship program was the final straw for the area and for an industry which has been neglected and discriminated against far too often by an uncaring Government.
Despite the fact that there are three Liberal Members who represent the Niagara region, that area was overlooked and bypassed by the 1LAP program. The response from the Minister remained that the Niagara region was being monitored closely. We are now being tantalized by a program which calls the area a qualifying centre for special Tier 1 designation.
Following on ILAP came the Industrial and Regional Development Program designed to promote industrial renewal and modernization in areas where long-term employment strategies are needed. Unemployment rates are said to account for 50 per cent of the weight when assigning tier designations.
St. Catharines-Niagara was given a tier one rating, the lowest possible. Mr. Speaker, there can hardly be much credibility in an employment program when the area with the highest urban unemployment in Canada fails to qualify for meaningful assistance.
What is more, the Government's own bureaucrats point out in a confidential report to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), that meaningful recovery in St. Catharines, utilizing the existing local economic base, cannot occur. It went on to say that "it is within the urban centres of southwestern Ontario and the Niagara Peninsula that much of the industrial renewal and export development efforts will need to be directed." Those views and conclusions, Mr. Speaker, were submitted to the Minister last February.
How well received was that economic advice? From that time, the Niagara region has essentially been bypassed in the Special Recovery Capital Projects; it has received the lowest possible tier designation for the IRDP; it did not receive any LEAD funding and no shipbuilding contracts.
Consequently, when 1 hear Minister after Minister talking about bold initiatives to combat unemployment, I am led to ask-where? Why are unemployment needs elsewhere addressed more rapidly than in Niagara?
1 am struck by the irony of the Minister's response. After having been granted a contract, a further $2.2 million advance had to be made for yard improvement, but the Minister says that there is no relationship. It all depends upon who is signing the contracts. That money was advanced at least in part for shipyard renovation. Without that renovation, the bid on the icebreaker contract from Marine Industries might well have been higher. Indeed, Marine Industries received two icebreaker contracts. Fair is fair.
I would like to know which to believe as between the Minister's statement in the House that the lowest bid is the only criterion and the news release from his office which gives consideration to socio-economic factors. Which is it?

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul-Andre Masse (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-CRITERIA GOVERNING CONTRACTS- UNEMPLOYMENT AT PORT WELLER. (B) SUBSIDY TO MARINE INDUSTRIES IN SOREL, P.Q.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the concern of the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) and I will do my best to lay to rest his doubts about the policy on Government contracts.
I would like to point out that between May and September 1983, Port Weller Dry Dock Limited was invited six times to submit tenders for the construction or refitting of ships belonging to the Government of Canada. Unfortunately, the tenders submitted by the company failed to win any of the contracts. 1 may add that it was mainly on the basis of the principle of the lowest bidder that the Port Weller proposals were not chosen. As the House is aware, this is one of the basic rules of our policy on Government contracts.
1 also may remind the House that the concern for regional balance which was maintained in awarding the contracts demonstrates the Government's clear intention to act in the best interests of the country and its various regions.
The point I am trying to make is that Port Weller was not in any way discriminated against, compared to other Canadian shipyards. Moreover, the company was able to benefit from assistance under the Shipbuilding Industry Assistance Program administered by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley).
To get back to the criterion of the lowest bidder, I would like to add the following information. In May 1983, Port Weller Dry Dock submitted the highest of ten tenders received for the construction of a 72-metre patrol boat. In June 1983, we had the same situation for the construction of a 69-metre hydrographic survey ship, and during the same month. Port Weller Dry Dock refused to submit a tender for refitting the HMCS Protecteur, since its technical department could not handle any more work.
In July 1983, Port Weller Dry Dock submitted the fourth highest tender out of six from Eastern Canada-and only from Eastern Canada-for the construction of the type 1100 icebreakers.
In September 1983, Port Weller submitted the ninth highest tender out of ten for replacement of gas turbines and modifications to be made on the ship Norman McLeod Rogers. Finally, Port Weller submitted the highest of six tenders received for the refitting of the Sir Humphrey Gilbert. On Tuesday, November 15, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Lapointe), his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) and the Member for Welland (Mr. Parent) met with representatives of the company and the unions to examine the situation. Together they considered various contracts the Government would be letting to shipyards within the foreseeable future, and for which Port Weller would be asked to submit tenders. Mr. Speaker, I hope this answers satisfactorily
November 28, 1983

the question raised by my hon. colleague from St. Catharines, and I hope the Niagara region will continue to benefit from the Government of Canada's recovery program.
