EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CYPRUS-DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE BY TURKISH CYPRIOTS. (B) SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN AMBASSADOR FROM ANKARA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent declaration of independence on the part of the Turkish Cypriot community is a matter of grave concern to Greek Cypriot Canadians in my riding, Broadview-Greenwood. My predecessor, Bob Rae, took a great interest in the Cyprus issue, raised these as concerns forcefully in the House and defended the continuing Canadian presence of our peacekeeping forces in Cyprus. I intend to carry on in the same way to raise Cyprus issues, new and old, as long as is necessary.
The Cypriot Federation of Canada has made clear what it considers needs to be done. Let me quote:
We condemn without reservation the Denktash regime for its illegal declaration of independence of the Turkish occupied part of Cyprus. We call upon the Canadian Government to do whatever necessary to nullify this breach of the London-Zurich Agreement including the imposition of sanctions on the Denktash regime and on the Turkish Government, which is responsible first for the invasion in 1974 and now the attempt at illegal partition of the Republic of Cyprus. We further ask the Canadian Government to condemn this illegal declaration of independence in all appropriate international forums of which Canada is a member.
Well, Canada has condemned this action. It has protested diplomatically. The Government has made clear it will not recognize the pseudo state so illegally declared. Canada has spoken strongly at the United Nations; all this is to the good, but it is not enough.
On November 17 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) if he would show the disapproval of our Canadian people of the Turkish government's role in recognizing the new regime, such as by withdrawing our ambassador to Turkey. This has been a request of the Cypriot Federation of Canada, among other organizations.
The Minister's reply was wholly unsatisfactory. He noted that the Turkish government has stated it was not behind the unilateral declaration of independence. So be it. But the Turkish government was the first to recognize the illegal regime, despite its responsibility in guaranteeing an independent Cyprus back in 1960. The Turkish government should not have recognized the new regime. Indeed it should have told the Denktash regime to withdraw that declaration.
It is well known that intercommunal difficulties in Cyprus are of long standing. Nevertheless there has been a considerable time in which the two communities have lived fairly well and peacefully side by side. I believe it can happen again, but not while one community has the Armed Forces of another country to back it up.
The sad fact is that Cyprus was invaded in 1974 by Turkish armed forces. The result is that 18 per cent of the population is occupying 40 per cent of the land mass. Some 6,000 Greek
Adjournment Debate
Cypriots were killed in the war of invasion. There are 200,000 Greek Cypriots who are refugees from their homes, and some thousands of Turkish Cypriots had to go in the opposite direction. Turkey now has some 25,000 soldiers on Cyprus. About 2,000 Greek Cypriots are still missing from the war of invasion. There have been sightings of these people. There is enough to suggest that some, if not many, are still alive in camps in Turkey.
On October 3, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to put pressure on the Turkish government to seek release of these people as a humanitarian concern. The Minister replied that he would investigate. He subsequently said he would not take any action on behalf of Canada. He did not consider it appropriate for Canada on grounds of our role as a member of the peacekeeping forces. In my view this answer is inadequate. The people are still missing, we have reason to believe they are in Turkey, and the pressure has to be put on there.
The Minister said in his letter that a solution to the problem of missing persons in Cyprus will only be possible through an ongoing dialogue between the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, and that in view of the sensitive relations between the two sides this issue can be dealt with most effectively through appropriate UN channels or intercommunal talks rather than on a bilateral basis. 1 do not agree, Mr. Speaker. UN channels have been tried for years. Naturally we should continue but further action is also needed.
This is not just a Greek-Turkish Cypriot problem. The missing persons have been seen in Turkey, another country, not in Turkish occupied Cyprus. They were captured by the Turkish Army. In keeping a strict neutrality on Cyprus affairs, Canada has been too neutral, in my opinion. The missing Greek Cypriots constitute a humanitarian issue on which any country should feel free, indeed duty bound, to speak. Yet Canada abstained on the UN resolution on the grounds of its participation in the peacekeeping forces. Other peacekeeping participants have taken positions on the missing persons issue, including Australia, Austria, Denmark, Finland and Sweden, without hampering their effectiveness.
Cyprus is a situation in which there is an aggressor and a victim. No one is suggesting there is an equal number of Turkish Cypriots missing in Greece. The Cypriots are being held in camps on Turkish territory. Turkey is a much larger and more powerful country with a massive standing army. When it comes to an issue like missing persons, a human rights issue, we must not let some arbitrary principle rule. We must stand up and speak forcefully on a matter of injustice.
On the issue of Canadian peacekeeping forces, I was pleased to see the reassurance on the part of the Canadian Government to keep our forces in Cyprus. We need them there as long as foreign troops are on the island. At the same time I must express considerable concern with the statement made by the Conservative critic on external affairs. That spokesperson has used the latest crisis to raise the possibility of Canada with-

November 28, 1983
Adjournment Debate
drawing our peacekeeping contribution. In my view this is the worst time we should be raising this issue. Certainly we want to get our troops home, but only when the need no longer exists.
I am sorry to have to note the Conservative hypocrisy on this matter. On Sunday, November 20, I spoke at a rally organized by the Cypriot Federation of Canada in Toronto to protest the illegal declaration of independence. The Conservative representative at that rally said the Conservative Party was with the Greek Cypriot community, but where is it when we have to talk about peacekeeping forces? They have either been silent or on the wrong side.
To conclude, I just want to express the concern of all Canadians to the families of people who have members missing or refugees. We will continue to work to see that these people are returned to their homes. I will certainly, and 1 can speak for my Party, continue to work for justice in Cyprus.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paui-Andre Masse (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CYPRUS-DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE BY TURKISH CYPRIOTS. (B) SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN AMBASSADOR FROM ANKARA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really did not intend to monopolize the adjournment debate today. Nevertheless, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), 1 shall be glad to answer the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mrs. McDonald).
The position of the Government of Canada on recent events in Cyprus was made very clear in statements made in the House by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs, and more recently by Canada's intervention in the UN Security Council. The Government of Canada deplores the unilateral declaration of independence of the so-called Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, made on November 15, 1983. Canada recognizes only one Cypriot state, the Republic of Cyprus, and it has no intention of recognizing the new state that was proclaimed unilaterally. We firmly support action
being taken by the Secretary General of the UN with a view to reconciling the Greek and Turkish communities in Cyprus. The unilateral declaration of independence by Turkish Cypriots can only obstruct such action and compromise any chances of arriving at a fair and durable settlement.
When we intervened in the debate on Cyprus on November 15, in the UN Security Council, we reiterated our firm support for the efforts of the Secretary General to arrive at a negotiated settlement and urged other countries to do the same. The resolution adopted by the Security Council clearly reflects international reaction to recent events in Cyprus. In addition to its intervention in the UN, Canada has made its position known to the parties directly concerned by the Turkish Cypriot proclamation, including the Governments of Turkey, Greece and Cyprus. Turkish Ministers stated that the unilateral declaration of independence had taken place without the consent or knowledge of their Government. Nevertheless, Canada expressed its concern about the recognition by Turkey of the new Cypriot state and asked the Turkish Government to use its influence on Turkish Cypriot leaders in order to promote a settlement of this dispute.
The Government of Cyprus has, in fact, expressed its satisfaction with Canada's attitude. Canada, which for nearly twenty years has taken part in the United Nations peacekeeping forces in Cyprus, is very anxious to see a negotiated settlement. The Government of Canada believes it is essential that there should again be a dialogue between the two communities, and we shall do our best to make this happen. However, we do think a measure of the kind suggested by the Hon. Member would bring about a reconciliation between the two parties.
